maps.title: 2010 Shrimp Bait Formula
maps.text:
Shrimp Bait Formula 
by John Martinis-John’s Sporting Goods 
 
 
 
Items needed:  
Friskies Ocean White Fish w/ Tuna canned cat food 
Bumble Bee canned Mackerel 
Super Bait Prawn Bait pellets 
Pro Cure Shrimp Attractant Oil 
6” bait barrel  
 
The idea of mixing all these ingredients together is to set up a scent trail to attract shrimp 
to your shrimp pot.  Once the shrimp are near your pot, there is a good chance that they 
will want to enter the pot and feed on the Mackerel and pellets.  The cat food and the Pro 
Cure shrimp oil will quickly leach out of the pot and attract shrimp.  The pellets and the 
Mackerel will keep the shrimp in the pot once they get inside.  You can see the purpose 
of the different ingredients.   
 
Some people like to mix all the ingredients together and freeze the mixture in a large bait 
barrel.  They put the frozen mixture in the pot and let it un-thaw while the pot is working.  
Some people will add ground up fish to the mixture and others will add dry cat food 
(Friskies Seafood Sensation). 
 
My recommendation per pot:  
1) Put 3 cups of Super Bait shrimp bait pellets in a zip lock bag and add 1 cup of Pro 
Cure shrimp Attractant Oil in the zip lock bag.  Soak the pellets for one hour 
before shrimping. 
2) After the pellets soak for one hour, put the pellets in the 6” bait barrel.  Hang the 
bait barrel from the inside of the shrimp pot. 
3) Poke holes in one can of Mackerel and insert the can in the center bait 
compartment in the shrimp pot. 
4) Poke holes in 2 cans of Friskies Ocean White Fish w/ Tuna and insert the cans in 
the center bait compartment in the shrimp pot 
5)  Lets the shrimp pot over board and soak the pot for 45-60 minutes. 
 
Each time you let the shrimp pot out and retrieve it, you need to replace the canned cat 
food.  It pretty much washes out of the cans fairly fast.  The pellets will last all day and 
the canned Mackerel will last most of day.  The cat food is the only item that needs 
frequent replacing. 
 
I have recommended this concoction to many shrimp anglers and they find that it works 
quite well.  Some anglers will just use the pellets; other anglers will use only the canned 
Mackerel.  Use it all to set up that good scent trail. 
 
Click here for shrimp gear and bait

San Juan’s Area 7
Show me the Money
Marine Area 7 opens December 1 and it 
cannot come fast enough for Puget 
Sound saltwater salmon anglers.   If 
everyone feels like I do, I can't wait to 
get a crack at some decent size Chinook.  
I don't expect fishing to be like it was 
this summer.  With a little luck, there 
should be good fishing in the usual 
places like Rosario Straits, the Banks and 
the North end of Orcas Island.
This is what I anticipate from past 
experiences: If you want larger Chinook, 
then you have to fish Tide Point, Eagle 
Bluff, Reef Point, Parker Reef or 
McArthur Bank.  Hein Bank, Eastern 
Bank and Partridge will have lots of 
salmon but not many over 10 pounds. 
You notice I did not mention Eagle Point 
on the west side of San Juan Islands 
where there was decent fishing this 
summer.  I just don't think there will be 
big fish coming out of this area in 
December.
Now, we have to talk about the 
u p c o m i n g  s a l m o n  D e r b i e s : 
Resurrection Derby December 4th and 
5th with a $10,000 first Prize. The Friday 
Harbor Salmon Classic, also on 
December 4th and 5th, likewise has a 
$10,000 Prize.  That's $20,000 up for 
grabs for a two day period.  Now, here is 
the problem; where to go, what to use 
and will bait or hardware get the 
winning fish?
Links to Derbies 
Resurrection Derby 
Friday Harbor Classic
Before you start thinking about fishing 
the Derbies, consider the tides.  Tides 
are a constant influence in the San Juan 
Islands and one must use this as a 
dependable indicator for successful 
salmon fishing.
On both days, December 4th and 5th, 
the tides are almost the same.  
December 4th, the first daylight tide will 
be a High tide at 11:44 AM.  Then the 
tide goes out for the rest of the day until 
Low tide at 7:17 PM.   December 5th, 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
High tide is 12:15 PM and Low at 7:48 
PM.  Both days the tide comes in at 
daylight and High tide will linger to 
about Noon.  From Noon, (both days) 
t h e  t i d e  w i l l  e b b .   W i t h  t h i s 
information, one has to decide where 
to go for that $10,000 salmon.  
When you are fishing a particular area 
in the San Juan's, take a look at what is 
going on around you.  Look for current 
seams on the surface of the water.  A 
current seam will be a break between 
the fast water and the slower water.  
This will be an area where bait and 
Chinook will be found.  Most fish like 
to travel in those current seams 
because that is where they find their 
source of food. Don't find yourself 
fishing in the faster water.  Fish have 
to conserve energy, so they like to take 
the easier route at the edge of the 
current.  This is one of the most useful 
tips that I can give to someone fishing 
in Rosario Straits.  This summer when 
I was fishing at Eagle Point on the west 
side of San Juan Island, most days I 
found my best fishing for Chinook in 
sixty feet of water.  This was well 
inside the current seam that ran off of 
Eagle Point.  I used the same strategy 
a t  M i d  C h a n n e l  B a n k  a t  Po r t 
Townsend in July.  I fished in sixty feet 
of water when the tide was running 
hard.  Once again these techniques 
paid off big time.  Two very different 
places, same results. Chinook in the 
boat each time. 
I am not making a case for fishing in 
sixty feet of water, I am making a case 
for fishing inside the current seam.  
The water runs slower in the daylight 
hour during the winter months, so the 
current seam could inside of 90-120 
feet deep at most places.
Here are a few fishing suggestions 
concerning the December 4th and 5th 
tides.  Keep in mind this advice 
applies to any day in the San Juan 
Islands when tides are identical to the 
4th and 5th.  Before Noon each day I 
would fish Eagle Bluff on the North 
end of Cypress Island, Parker Reef on 
the North end of Orcas Island or Rocky 
Bay on the East side of San Juan Island.
When the Noon tide starts ebbing, the 
entire game plan changes.  In the 
afternoon, on both days, I would 
probably fish Tide Point on the West 
side of Cypress Island, Reef Point (on 
the South end of Cypress Island), 
Lopez Flats and Mc Arthur Bank.  
There are other more productive 
areas for Chinook fishing, but this 
gives you a starting point.

Effective San Juan Bait and 
Tackle Rigs
This summer when fishing the San 
Juan's, I frequently changed rigs so 
that I could offer fish some variety.  On 
one rod I had a fish flasher and bait 
and on another rod I had flashers and 
spoons.  The latter accomplished two 
things: The flasher and spoon combo 
was unlikely to hook up shaker “bait 
robbers” and the “spoon combo” 
spent more time in the water fishing.  
The flasher and bait rig still offered 
fish something like the bait they were 
chasing.  However, sometimes, we 
didn't fish bait since it was just too 
much trouble.  If you get into a really 
good shaker bite, it is a better not to 
fish bait since you tend to lose quality 
fishing time.  So, this is the choice that 
has to be made every day.  However, 
always bring Herring or Anchovies and 
start the day with at least one rig 
hooked up with bait.
During the winter months in the San 
Juan's, I found smaller spoons work 
the best.  The Goldstar 3.0 Kingfisher 
and the Goldstar Coho Killer Spoons 
are good choices.  Rig either spoon 42 
inches behind a flasher. Leaders can 
be as long as 60 inches.  Use these 
colors of spoons: Cookies n Cream 
#975, Red Racer #964 and the New 
Herring Aide color #395.
Using Herring or Anchovies
When rigging a flasher with either 
Herring or Anchovies, I recommend 
the Gibbs Farr Better Flasher (Sliding 
Flasher).  Use a Rhys Davis Anchovy 
Special Head (Clear UV or Chrome) 
with a 60 inch leader tied to a flasher.  
This is an effective rig when used with 
5 inch herring or anchovy in the Head 
holder.

items to see what they look like.

December 
Dungeness Crab
If you have not been out crabbing, you 
are missing out on one of the better 
winter crab seasons in some time.  
Not only are the crab larger than 
normal, they are in good supply.  If 
you are heading out, I recommend 
someplace around the Hat Island 
(Gedney Island) area.  The Northwest 
corner of Hat Island has been good 
crabbing as well as the eastern side of 
the Island.  On the east side of Hat 
Island there is a bar that extends 
towards Everett.  Set your pots in 50 
to 75 feet of water.  On the Northwest 
corner of Hat Island, do the same 
thing.
Crabbing Map
Hat Island Crab Map
Areas 8-1 and 8-2 
Chinook
High winds and muddy water have put 
a temporary hold on Areas 8-1 and 8-2 
Chinook fishing.  When water clarity 
returns to normal (it might happen by 
the time you read this), typical fishing 
should return for this time of year.
Winter Chinook fishing has not been 
robust but anglers putting in an extra 
effort are getting decent Chinook to 
the boat.  This isn't rock'm-sock'm 
fishing.  This is grinding it out for a 
decent Chinook each day.
I have three recommendations for 
December Areas 8-1 and 8-2 Chinook 
fishing: The bar running between Hat 
Island and Camano Island, Elger Bay 
and Onamac Point.  Both Elger Bay 
and Onamac Point are off Camano 
Island.
Tackle references for these areas 
include recommendations I made for 
Area 7 fishing except using 3.5 
Kingfisher spoons.  My thoughts for 
using larger spoons are larger bait fish 
found in Puget Sound this time of year 
compared to the San Juan's. 
Area 9 Opening?
According to the Sport Fishing Rule 
Book (page 119), the next Area 9 
Chinook opening will be January 16.  I 
don't have any insider information 
about possible date changes, but I 
believe fishing will start on that date. 
Where it goes from there nobody 
truly knows.  There is a chance that 
the November flood waters entering 
Puget Sound have pushed the sub-
legal Chinook further to the west and 
into the Straits of Juan de Fuca.  
Hopefully these “sub-legal” fish are 
gone from Area 9 and there can be 
normal winter Chinook fishing 
starting January 16.

Winter Chinook Fishing
The winter solstice is approaching 
(December 22) and the salmon seasons 
are changing along with the weather 
change.  Right now, the Coho season is 
wrapping up and we are preparing for 
winter Chinook fishing in Puget Sound 
and San Juan Islands.  
One thing that is also going to change is 
the Chinook regulations/seasons.  
Because of the Chinook mortality rate 
from the Chinook encounters in 
September and October, I believe the 
WDFW will impose some regulations 
using season length/dates or tackle 
restriction so that we can keep fishing 
but having fewer impacts on juvenile 
Chinook (sub legal Chinook/shakers).  I 
don't have that information yet, so I 
would consider all possibilities so that 
you can adjust to any new rules which 
could be made near the November 1, 
Puget Sound Chinook season opening.
Go to this link on the WDFW web site to 
get all the saltwater emergency 
regulation updates, .Click Here
I would be prepared for a regulation 
that imposes gear restrictions such as 
using salmon plugs.  We can all live with 
this:  A five inch plug with a 5/0 siwash 
hook is lethal for winter Chinook.  Plugs 
that are very effective for Chinook are 
Scotty 1106 $473
Click Here to Order
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
Tomic 602 and 603 five inch plugs.  I 
also like the five inch Silver Horde 
plugs in white or purple haze.  When I 
first began my career in the fishing 
business, all I used were five inch 
white Silver Horde Plugs for salmon 
fishing.  That's what everyone used to 
catch Chinook at one time. Needless 
to say, times have changed and so has 
salmon tackle.  One aspect of fishing 
with plugs I really enjoy, is a lack of 
sub-legal Chinook that are caught.  
This maximizes my fishing time and 
allows me to catch larger Chinook.  
Think about that for a moment.  Every 
minute your gear is out of the water 
releasing sub-legal Chinook, is a 
minute wasted.  During the Coho 
season my gear was out of the water 
probably 30% of the time because of 
the intense shaker bite just about 
everywhere I fished in Puget Sound.
Rigging Plugs
There are two methods for rigging 
plugs.  With Tomic or Silver Horde 
Plugs, tie the plug right to the end of 
the fishing line.  Some anglers prefer 
using 3 to 4 feet of 30 pound leader 
tied to a ball bearing swivel when 
using plugs.  Both methods are good.  
Never attach a snap swivel to the plug 
since that will ruin the plug action.
If and when the gear regulations are 
lifted, we can then go back to a variety 
of gear which we accustomed to 
using.  Or, just stick with the plugs 
with hopes of catching larger Chinook.  
At my Coho seminar, I introduced the 
Gibbs Farr Better flasher to many of 
you for the first time. The Gibbs Farr 
Better flasher is a release type flasher 
similar to the Qcove flasher.  I use this 
flasher almost exclusively with 
herring and I use it with what I call 
“unplugged”.  I don't plug the red pin 
into the flasher.  I simply let the 
flasher rotate around the flasher 
harness.  Unplugged the flasher will 
rotate around the supplied flasher 
harness just like a spinner blade.  You 
ask yourself, “What's the advantage of 
this?”  This is one of the most potent 
ways to use a flasher and herring that 
personally I have ever seen.  A side 
benefit is that I don't get any leader 
malfunctions when I hook-up a nice 
Chinook.  I experience no leader 
breaks while using the Gibbs Farr 
Better Flasher unplugged.  Earlier in 
the year when fishing Partridge Bank 
and Eastern Bank, I lost three nice 
Chinook from leader breaks using a 
standard flasher and spoon.  I am 
eager to use the Farr Better Flasher 
unplugged with spoons this winter 
when fishing for Chinook.  Give it a try, 
I believe that you will like it.  Watch 
this video I made on how to rig the 
Gibbs Farr Better Flasher: Click Here 
When I am using spoons for Chinook, I 
like using the Goldstar 3.5 Kingfisher 
spoons #964 and 975.  I like this spoon 
not only for the color, but for the way 
it is rigged.  This spoon has a good 
quality stainless Mustad siwash hook 
on a swivel.  This hook will never 
break and the hook point will remain 
sharp for many fishing trips.  I 
recommend a 42 inch leader from the 
flasher to the spoon.  Use 30 pound 
Pline fluorocarbon leader material to 
tie the spoon to the flasher.
Two flashers that I exclusively use and 
strongly recommend are the Gibbs 
11” UVGRMJRS flasher (Red Racer) 
and the Gibbs 11” PUSUV Flasher 
(Purple Haze).  Hot Spot flashers are 
also effective, they simply are more 
expensive.  
Quite a few Coho anglers have come 
in the store with twisted line 
problems.  One thing they all had in 
common was the fact that they were 
not using American Made Sampo Ball 
Bearing swivels.  I know these swivels 
are expensive, I hear that.  These 
swivels end the frustration of line 
t w i st  w h e n  u s i n g  f l a s h e rs .   I 
recommend the Sampo X3CB snap 
swivel tied to the end of the fishing 
line.  Snap the flasher onto the line 
with the X3CB snap swivel.

During the Coho season there were 
always little clues on where to fish for 
winter Chinook.  For example; I 
recently caught and released a 12 
pound Chinook on the most southern 
end of Possession Bar while I was 
fishing Coho.  I talked to Coho anglers 
who regularly caught legal size 
Chinook from Indian Point to the 
Scatchet Head Buoy.  I feel that there 
is a good number of larger than just 
barely legal size Chinook roaming 
around Possession Bar.
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
Now, you have to change your fishing 
habits from roaming around looking 
for Coho to a somewhat technical 
method for Chinook fishing.  Let me 
unlock some of these secrets to a 
successful Chinook trip.
Chinook anglers who are skilled at 
depth control are those who regularly 
catch fish.  You probably have friends 
or co-workers that go out and catch 
Chinook with a high degree of 
regularity.  Many anglers quit fishing 
after the Coho season runs its course 
because the Chinook seems to be too 
elusive target for them.  Face it, going 
out and coming back to the dock with 
no fish just does not produce the 
same thrill as a 10 to 12 pound 
Chinook peeling line off the reel.  
After catching 3 and 4 pound Coho, I 
was thrilled to catch and release a 12 
pound Chinook. For a moment I 
thought I was in Sitka again.  Reality 
check?  
You can control the depth at which 
you are fishing using two different 
methods or a combination of the two: 
Control the boat so that you stay in 
the desired depth range.  Move the 
downrigger up and down like yo-yo.  I 
like the more modest approach by 
keeping the boat at the depth I wish to 
be in and then making subtle 
adjustments to the downrigger 
depth.  Sounds like work?  It is!  
Learn to fish contours for Chinook. 
Chinook feed on the breaking edges of 
contour lines.  Let's use Possession 
Bar for an example.  You will find the 
best but not all the most productive 
Chinook fishing in 90 to 120 feet of 
water.  Why?  That is where the edges 
of the Bar break quickly before the Bar 
descends rapidly to 500 to 700 feet of 
water.  Where's the bait?  Most 
frequently along those edges and 
breaks in the Bar.  Sure, you can catch 
a Chinook wandering around in no 
man's land.  Attempts to repeat that 
drill time after time and you will wear 
out rather quickly.  Learn to fish the 
edges and the angles of any place that 
you fish.  By angles I mean where 
there is a sharp turn in the Bar or 
some subtle protruding tip in the Bar.  
Look for this stuff while you are 
fishing.  Try to make sense of why and 
where the bait/Chinook are hanging 
out.  What you will find is, time after 
time you can rely on these areas to 
produce Chinook.  When I fish for 
Chinook, I fish actual spots.  I try to get 
my boat in position ahead of time so 
that I know that I am going to troll by 
the bottom structure that I know 
holds bait and Chinook.  If you are just 
starting out, this is going to be little 
more difficult until you put in your 
time and log some results.  
Chinook Speed
Time to slow down.  The best Chinook 
speeds are between 2.5 and 3.0 mph.  
Nearer that 2.5 mph range works 
better for me.  Remember while you 
are adjusting the speed, you also need 
to adjust the downrigger depth.  
Don't get complacent and not let 
more downrigger cable out if you 
increase you speed.  Fishing close to 
the bottom always produces more 
Chinook over a long period of time. 
So far, I think I have given you some 
good advice which you can use just 
about anywhere.

If you have not heard, the squid 
population has exploded lately in 
Puget Sound.  Squid fishing at the 
Seattle Elliott Bay Fishing Pier at 
Terminal 86 has been outstanding 
with any Squid anglers getting limits.  
The Edmonds fishing has also been 
g o o d  b u t  n o t  w i t h  t h e  s a m e 
consistency as Pier 86. Regulations: 
No size limit, Daily limit 5 quarts or 10 
pounds, maximum four squid lures.
Here is a useful on how to fish for 
squid, .Click Here
Puget Sound
Dungeness Crab 
Most Areas in Puget Sound are open for 
Dungeness crab until the end of 
December.  From the information that I 
am getting, the crabbing has been quite 
good.  Most of the Crabbers are finding 
the best depths are between 75 and 125 
feet deep.  Use some of those Coho 
carcasses for bait and turn them into a 
crab dinner.  I would recommend 
crabbing in these areas: Shipwreck to 
Picnic Point and the north side of Hat 
Island (Gedney Island).

Halibut Clinic
April 21
By John Martinis
You are invited to my Halibut Clinic. I will 
discuss all the methods new and old 
that I talk about in this Newsletter.  
Please join me at the Everett Salmon 
and Steelhead Club on April 21, @7PM.  
The Halibut clinic is free to the public.  
Click Here for Directions
HOOKED ON 
HALIBUT 
I want to start the Halibut round-up 
early because I am completely addicted 
to Halibut fishing.
Here are the Halibut Seasons for Areas 5 
through 10.
Western Region (Marine Area 5): Open 
Saturday, May 7; Thursday through 
Saturday, May 12 - 14; and Thursday 
through Sunday May 26 - 29.
Eastern Region (Marine Areas 6, 7, 8, 9 
and 10) (Marine Areas 11 - 13 are 
closed): Open Saturday, May 7; 
Thursday through Saturday, May 12 - 
14; and Thursday through Sunday May 
26 - 29.
I caught my first 2016 Halibut on March 
22 on the Canadian Side of Coyote Bank. 
This year I am planning a Halibut trip to 
Sitka, Queen Charlotte Islands and 
Washington State.  I am addicted to 
these big flatfish!  What drives my 
passion for a fish that has both eyes on 
the same side of the head? Halibut are 
an exciting fish to catch.  A Halibut bite 
at the end of a fishing line could deliver 
a 12-pound fish or a chance for a 
possible 100-pound giant.
I caught three Halibut since January 1st.  
Two were caught while salmon fishing 
and released and a 45-pound Halibut 
was caught in Canada which I retained.  
The first Halibut was approximately 40 
pounds and caught on a Coho Killer 
Spoon.  I caught the next Halibut a week 
later on a 5-inch Herring. Both were 
caught on Partridge Bank while salmon 
fishing.  The next Halibut was caught on 
March 22nd on a 9-inch white plastic 
squid with a salmon belly on the hook.  
Do you see a trend developing?  Well, 
there is none.  These three Halibut were 
caught on entirely different types and 
sizes baits. Two were caught trolling and 
one caught while anchored.  They were

all caught using a downrigger.  That's 
right, downrigger fishing for Halibut.
During the 2015 Halibut season and 
the 2016 Halibut year, I caught more 
Halibut using a downrigger than using 
1 to 2 pounds of lead on the end of a 
f i s h i n g  l i n e .  T h e r e  i s  s t i l l  a 
requirement to fish both methods 
and I will explain that as we go.
Let's first address being anchored and 
Halibut fishing with a downrigger.  For 
myself, I just got tired of using a 2-
pound weight on the end of my line 
when the tide was running hard.  My 
thought was:  I already have a chum 
b a g  o u t  a n d  a t t a c h e d  t o  m y 
downrigger ball.  Why not just attach 
a downrigger release one foot above 
the downrigger ball and fish for 
Halibut like I would for salmon?  The 
only real difference is that I now am 
anchored rather than trolling.  That 
makes a lot of sense to me.  I tried this 
on Hein Bank last year and caught 
most my Halibut using the downrigger 
method.
Let me explain the Halibut downrigger 
fishing method: Assuming you are 
using 65 pound braided fishing line, 
tie a 100-pound test barrel swivel to 
the end of the 65 pound braided 
fishing line.  
Tie a Halibut leader using 60 to 80-
pound leader material and two 10/0 
Gamakatsu Hooks.  Tie the hooks to 
accommodate a 7 to 8-inch herring 
and make the leader 4 feet in length.  
Leader tying tip; I have been installing 
a small chunk of glow rubber tubing 
between the two 10/0 Gamakatsu 
hooks so that my leaders have more 
resistance to dog fish teeth. See 
photo, Click Here
Slide a corky or large bead down the 
leader as a squid insert.  In place of 
the corky or large bead I often use fat 
yarn.  The yarn is used to absorb the 
herring oil that I apply. Tie the fat yarn 
just above the eye of the upper hook.
Slide a 7 to 9-inch white squid down 
the leader.  The squid can also be slid 
down the leader upside down.  If you 
slide the squid down upside down, do 
not use a corky or bead. Just tie the fat 
yarn above the eye of the hook. Now 
tie the leader to the 100-pound test 
swivel.  See Photo, Click Here
Anytime I am using a 7 to 9-inch 
plastic squid, I always use a 7 to 8-inch 
herring or a piece of salmon belly for 
bait.  Either bait is tied to the leader 
with miracle thread.  Don't skimp on 
the thread.  Tie the bait on so it will 
not come off the leader under any 
circumstances. 
Let the fishing line out 25 feet behind 
the downrigger.  Attach the fishing 
line to a downrigger release.  Let the 
downrigger ball down until it touches 
bottom and then crank the ball up 6 
inches.
When you are fishing for Halibut with 
a downrigger, don't expect to see a 
strike that rips the fishing line out of 
the downrigger release.  No, no, no.  
The bite/strike will feel look like this: a 
simple bobbing motion of the fish rod 
tip or maybe the line will come out of 
the release as if the line released on its 
own. Wise Advice: Let the line 
become tight then strike hard!  Many 
times the bigger Halibut will inhale 
the whole bait and just hang on the 
end of the line.  Keep a sharp eye on 
the rod tip.
Fishing off a downrigger might seem 
to be the answer for Halibut fishing.  
Not so fast.  This method works well 
so long as water current is moving 
quickly. Once the water slows down 
this method does not work at all.  
That's right.  When the current slows 
down, fishing lines attached to the 
downriggers have a tendency to get 
tangled.  
When the water slows down, I switch 
back to using 1 to 2 pound weights.  I 
will go back to fishing off downriggers 
as soon as the water changes 
direction and velocity picks up.
Using weights and 
spreader bars
There are two excellent methods for 
Halibut rigging: spreader bars or 
Slydo.
Spreader Bar:  Tie leaders using 60 to 
80-pound leader material and two 
Gamakatsu 10/0 Hooks (same as 
above).  Make the leaders 24 inches 
long and install squid as I previously 
stated.  Tie the leader to the long arm 
of the spreader bar.  Use salmon belly 
or herring for bait.  Use rectangular 16 
t o  3 2  o u n c e  w e i g h t s .   T h e s e 
rectangular weights do not roll 
around in the boat and are more 
convenient to use.
Slydo Method:  A Slydo is nothing 
more than a plastic tube with a snap 
attached.  The snap is for attaching 
the weight.  Slide the Slydo on the 
main line.  Tie a 100-pound test barrel 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
swivel to the end of the line.  Use the 
same plastic squid and leader I 
mentioned earlier but make the 
leader 24 to 30 inches long.  Tie the 
leader to the 100-pound test barrel 
swivel.  Put the bait on the hooks.  
This method is really simple!
If you are using a spreader bar or Slydo 
for Halibut, you might be anchored or 
you might be drifting.  In either case, 
let the weight down to the bottom 
and gently swim the bait.  If you get 
tired of holding the rod with 2 pounds 
of weight on the end of the line, put 
the rod in the rod holder for a while.  If 
the rod has been in the rod holder for 
a 15 minutes, take the rod out and 
swim the bait.  Often Halibut might 
come near the bait but will not bite if 
it looks dead.  Once you jig the bait a 
nearby Halibut will jump at the 
chance at getting a live snack only to 
find out that he is now a tasty meal for 
you!
Capturing your catch
Be prepared to capture a large halibut 
if the opportunity comes your way. 
Most Halibut in the 12 to 30-pound 
range can be easily taken with a 
salmon net.  Halibut in the 30 to 60-
pound class can be gaffed.  Halibut 60 
pounds or larger need to be speared if 
you don't want to take a chance of 
losing a great catch.  In a nutshell: Be 
prepared for everything.
Netting: Simply lead a Halibut to the 
net much the way you do for salmon
Gaffing: Gaffing a Halibut can be a 
little tricky.  Sink the gaff into the head 
of the Halibut and bring the fish on 
board all in one motion.  Do not gaff 
the fish and hold it outside the boat to 
get a better look.  If you do, kiss the 
fish goodbye.  Once gaffed, Halibut 
twist and struggle with such strength 
that you can't hold onto the gaff or the 
fish will slip off of the gaff.  These fish 
simply are too wild to handle.
Spearing: Spearing is the ultimate 
way to capture a Halibut.  Once 
speared, it is highly unlikely that you 
will lose the fish.  Rig the spear with 20 
to 25 feet of 1/8-inch nylon cord and 
tie the cord to a cleat.  Spear the 
Halibut mid-body.  No Halibut meat 
will go wasted regardless of where 
you spear the fish.  Don't try to spear 
the Halibut in the head which is like 
stone and the spear tip might not go 
all the way through the fish.
It is not necessary to the tie the 1/8-
inch nylon cord to a buoy.  Spear the 
Halibut and get back to fishing as soon 
as possible because the bite is on if 
you just caught a halibut.  Use your 
fishing time wisely, because the 
season is only eight days long.  If you 
jack-ass around your next Halibut 
could be next year.

Technique That 
Matters
By Zack McGlothern
Zak is a very successful fishing 
guide that shops at John’s 
Sporting Goods.  Unlock the 
secrets of Kokanee Fishing and 
book a trip now with Zak.
Click Here to go to Zak’s website
Every year I find the Kokanee season 
begins earlier for me.  This last year we 
began chasing Kokanee in December 
with great success on several eastern 
Washington Lakes.  But the arrival of 
April means one thing, Kokanee 
season is here in full swing.  Lakes like 
Chelan and Roosevelt have been 
pumping out healthy Kokanee for 
months but soon my local Lakes such 
as Lake Stevens, Roesiger, Samish, 
Cavanaugh, and American will begin to 
warm into the Kokanee's preferred 
comfort range.  Most Kokanee anglers 
spend the winter months preparing 
for this time, and the time is coming 
soon.  But how do some anglers 
constantly produce limits of big 
Kokanee day after day? Or any fish for 
that matter.  How are they so 
consistent when there is nothing 
consistent about Kokanee fishing?  
Today I am going to share with you 5 
tips that have made me a better 
angler, for any species.
Organization and Cleanliness:  I know 
I am like many anglers, way to much 
fishing gear and it's all crammed into 
one tackle bag/box.  Keeping your 
gear clean and organized will help with 
clutter. But also will put more fish in 
the boat.  How many times have you 
found that lucky spinner in the bilge 
because it didn't get put away?  Or 
your hoochies are stuck together and 
formed a UV infused glue in your 
tackle box?  With a near constant 
influx of new gear into my collection, it 
has to find a spot.  For my lures I use 
every day I install them on pool 
noodles.  Most of these are 16” long 
and can hold enough gear to cover 
many of the Koke's moods.  I have one 
for my Spinners, Squids, and Flies.  It is 
easily accessible and when I remove 
my gear it doesn't get set on the table 
it gets put back on the roll, ready to 
fish again. This also allows my gear to 
dry and helps prevent rust.  I also carry 
several tackle boxes for dodgers and 
gear that hasn't been tested or just 
simply doesn't have my confidence.  
All leaders are ready to go and 
wrapped with a twist tie just in case 
the need arises and back up soldiers 
need to hit the battle field. Everything 
in my boat also has a place.  This keeps 
things off the floor and out of the way.  
At the end of the fishing day the gear, 
rods, and boat is washed and 
everything is put in its proper place for 
the next day.  This allows me to not 
worry about fishing the next day, and 
not where I put my lucky set up or 
where my pliers went to.  I also have 
my boat totally ready to go the night 
before I go fishing.  That way I am not 
forgetting anything at home the next 
day, like the net.... An organized 
fisherman is a successful fisherman.
P r e - p l a n  a n d  a c q u i r e  i n t e l :   
S o m e t i m e s  f i s h i n g  c a n  b e 
intimidating. Especially when fishing 
new water or new locations.  But lucky 
for many anglers we have the internet 
which allows us to connect with a 
network of anglers and information.  
Before I fish a new spot or new body of 
water I will dig up any piece of 
information I can find.  I will talk to my 
buddies and fellow guides who fish 
that water. Then I will establish a game 
plan. This will include where I am going 
to fish, depths, gear, scents, speed, 
and the times of day or tides that 
fishing can be productive.  Having this 
already set in your mind will prepare 
you for a successful day on the water.
Find fish:   All too often I hear of 
anglers have less then great days on 
the water, all because they fished one 
spot all day because it has produced 
fish before.  I find myself guilty of this 
as well.  Most successful fishermen 
are fishing with some kind of high end 
electronics with sonar.  If you are not, 
get one. This not only allows you see 
water depths but you can also see your 
target in the water column.  Now 
whether I am looking for bait to find 
Chinook, or looking for suspended 
Kokanee, my eyes are glued to my fish 
finder.  If I fish a spot I know holds fish 
for 30 minutes and I don't find them. I 
move. There is no point in trying to 
catch fish that aren't there.  Yes, you 
may hit a fish once in a while but you 
are fishing blind if you are not marking 
fish.  A properly tuned sonar will 
always mark fish if they are there.  
Once I do find fish I will refer to my GPS 
and try to stay on them as long as 
possible.  If you find a school of fish 
turn around and go back thru them.  If 
they don't want to bite change gear 
and try again. Targeting the depth the 
fish are at is also of the utmost 
importance.  I always try to run my 
downrigger 5 feet above the fish. Fish 
where the fish are, catch more fish.  
It's simple.
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
Change Gear and Re-scent/Rebait:   
Most fishermen have a pretty 
extensive collection of fishing tackle. I 
know I have more then I will ever use in 
my lifetime. But what good is all that 
tackle if you drag the same thing 
around all day with no success?  You 
have that tackle for a reason so use it!  
Many times while fishing I have found 
fish and had to change gear multiple 
times in order to get them to bite. 
Changing colors, profiles or action.  
Sometimes even a subtle change can 
trigger a full on bite.  Another error I 
have often seen (yes I am guilty too) is 
fishermen dragging around their gear 
for an hour or so without rebaiting or 
re-scenting.  Yes, I know it can be a 
pain pulling your gear up and setting it 
back out.   All too often it seems like 
the downrigger comes up and a school 
shows up on the sonar.  But scent is a 
very important part of most fisheries.  
So having fresh scent is very important 
as well!  Changing scents can also 
trigger non-willing fish to bite as well.  
Also, Kokanee are very fast.  Most can 
have your bait stripped off your hook 
before you know they are there and 
gone.  Trolling around without bait is 
going to make it hard to catch fish.  
Change gear and scent for non-willing 
fish, keep your bait and scent fresh. 
Got it? Good. Next!
Record Success:  You just spent a week 
planning your fishing trip. You had to 
grind on the water to find fish and get 
them to react.  In the end, fish were 
caught and a pattern was established.  
But what good is all that work if you 
don't remember what you did?  
Keeping record of what happened and 
really help with pre-planning trips and 
continuing success on the water.  I 
keep a fishing journal of every day I 
fish. I include things such as location, 
weather, depth, gear, scents, speed, 
and how productive I was.  All of this 
information leads to more consistent 
fishing no matter where I am fishing.  
Over several years I have been able to 
establish patterns on several bodies of 
water that I fish and this allows me to 
be a high percentage fishermen (most 
of the time).  Keep a record of what 
works, and what doesn't, and you will 
become a better angler.
In short, having a clean and organized 
boat will allow you to maximize your 
time on the water. Have a game plan 
before hitting the water and maybe 
even a backup plan. Use you sonar to 
find fish and if you aren't having 
success, then move! Keep your bait 
and scent fresh and change gear to 
trigger unwilling fish to bite.  And 
lastly, keep a record of all of your 
fishing, good or bad.  These fish tips 
h a v e  t u r n e d  m e  i n t o  a  g r e a t  
fishermen and have allowed me to 
turn my love for the outdoors into a 
professional career. Following these 
pointers will also help you put more 
fish in the box. Good luck out on the 
water everyone!

February Sage 
Salmon Advice
The Area 9 salmon season opening on 
J a n u a r y  1 6  s t a r t e d  w i t h  h u g e 
anticipation from a lot of salmon 
anglers since the October closure.  Even 
with the season opening, adverse 
weather conditions curbed a lot of 
angler's desire to fight high winds 
occurring throughout most of January.  
Hopefully February weather will be 
more promising.
What I did find out about the fishing this 
month was that most Puget Sound 
Chinook were just legal size to maybe 6 
or 7 pounds. I caught Chinook each time 
I went out but nothing of any size.  
I believe there are still a lot of legal 
hatchery Chinook to be caught in Puget 
Sound.  I say this since there has not 
been a lot of fishable days.  When

weather has an effect on the number 
of days we have on the water, fishing 
remains good for a longer time 
period.  There is just a certain amount 
of legal hatchery Chinook in the 
Sound at one time that are available.  
When the season is closed or the 
number of days available to fish are 
impacted by the weather, the 
population of catchable Chinook 
remains constant.  I believe this fact 
should hold true for February Chinook 
fishing.
In this month's Newsletter I want to 
cover Chinook fishing in Area 9 and in 
Area 8-1.  Just because Area 9 is open, 
it is not the only game in town.
Here's what is going on in Area 9.  If 
you want to catch larger Chinook, you 
need to head out to  Mid Channel Bank
at Port Townsend.  Mid Channel has 
been consistently producing larger 
fish.  Before heading in that direction 
take a look at the tide book.  This time 
of year the days are still fairly short.  
For that reason, it is nice to have a low 
tide between Noon and the end of the 
day.  If you are running to Mid 
Channel from Edmonds or the Everett 
area, you need start back to the dock 
by at least 2:30 pm to make it by 
sundown.  
At Mid Channel, fish on the ebb tide in 
90 to 100 feet of water and really close 
to the bottom.
Tackle I recommend for
 Mid Channel
˜Gibbs Red Racer flasher or Farr 
Better Flasher
˜#964 3.0 Kingfisher Spoon (Green 
Spatter Back w/Red Stripe)
˜#964 3.5 Kingfisher Spoon (Green 
Spatter Back w/Red Stripe)
˜#675 3.0 Kingfisher Spoon (Cookies 
n Cream)
˜# 395 3.0 Kingfisher Spoon (Herring 
Aide)
Fishing whole herring by itself or 
behind a flasher is also a basic staple 
for Chinook at Mid Channel.  If there 
are two of you fishing, I would start 
with a herring on one rig and a flasher 
and spoon on another rig.
Rig either size spoon 42 inches behind 
the flasher.  Fish herring 60 inches 
behind the flasher and insert the 
whole herring inside of a Rhys Davis 
Anchovy Specia l head (chrome or 
clear UV) with a 4 or 5 inch herring.  
Click here for an illustration on rigging 
the Rhys Davis Anchovy special.  The 
illustration is depicted using an 
anchovy.  Rig the herring using the 
same method.
There are fishing spots closer to the 
E d m o n d s / Ev e r e t t  a r e a  I  a l s o 
recommend when the tide is coming 
in for the next 28 days.  On a flood 
tide, fish Useless Bay.  I have been 
frequently fishing  and it Useless Bay
has been producing Chinook about 1 
½ hours before and up to high tide.  
There has not been much bait at 
Useless but the salmon fishing has 
been consistent.
While fishing Useless start trolling 
deep inside the Bay in front of the 
houses which has not been producing 
too many strikes.  The better Chinook 
fishing has been on the extreme 
southern end of the portion of the bar 
extending out from Double Bluff in 
depths of 100 to 125 feet.
Gear that has been working 
at Useless Bay
˜Coho Killer #675 Cookies and 
Cream)  
˜3.0 #675 Kingfisher Spoon (Cookies 
and Cream)
Fish either rig 42 inches behind a 
Gibbs Red Racer flasher (regular 
flasher or Farr Better Flasher).
Area 8-1 has also been solid Chinook 
fishing.  I mean catching at least one 
legal Chinook per day of fishing.  
The largest Chinook I have heard 
caught in the Sound since mid-
January was by Jeff Audett at Onamac 
Point (Camano Island) which topped 
the scales at 19 pounds.  You might 
have seen Jeff and his fish on John's 
Sporting Goods Facebook. 
In Area 8-1 there three places I 
recommend fishing
˜Green Bank
˜In Front of Camano Island State Park
˜Onamac Point
I have been catching my Chinook at 
Green Bank. While not great fishing, it 
has been turning out some legal 
Chinook on a regular basis.
Let me give you a good tip on fishing 
any of the three spots I suggested. 
Don't fish the typical 90 to 120 feet 
deep sections.  I have been fishing 65 
to 75 feet deep (water depth).  Jeff 
Audett has been successfully fishing 
50 to 55 feet of water.  This seems 
counterintuitive to what I normally 
recommend for fishing in Puget Sound 
but it works in these areas. 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
On the first trip I made to Green Bank, 
I could not find any bait in 90 to 120 
feet of water.  I had a total blue screen 
on the fish finder for the first two 
hours.   I got into shallow water by 
accident and found enormous schools 
of bait.  I stuck with the bait in 65 to 75 
feet of water and started catching 
fish.
W h e n  f i s h i n g  G r e e n  B a n k ,  I 
recommend fishing south of the 
houses on the beach.  Look for the 
large house with the tin roof on the 
bluff.  That's the spot.  Troll this area 
until you find bait and then stay on top 
of it the best you can.  The Chinook 
will not necessarily be on the bottom 
as normal.  Look for larger fish marks 
on your fish finder and fish those 
depths. 
Recently I talked to several Chinook 
anglers who do quite well right in 
front of Camano Island State Park.  
This is not in Elger bay, but right in 
front of the Park.  Fishing does not get 
any easier since there is no need to 
fire up the big motor on most days to 
fish this spo if you are launching your 
boat at the state park.  The good 
salmon fishing is right in front of the 
boat launch.
  
February Fishing Tip
If you want a simple and fast way to 
cure whole frozen herring try this. The 
night before, thaw herring out in the 
refrigerator.  In the morning coat them 
with Kosher rock salt.  I have found this 
works about as well as any of the more 
exotic herring cures.  I use this method 
whenever I use whole herring or in a Rhys 
Davis Anchovy head. On cool days there is 
no need to chill the herring.  On warmer 
days, put them on ice.
Spot Shrimp 
Success
OLYMPIA – Washington Department of 
Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) announced 
that recreational spot shrimp fishing in 
Puget Sound will open May 14 on a 
Saturday – one week later than usual. 
Shellfish managers are delaying the 
popular shrimp fishery until May 14 due 
to very low tides which are expected 
midday on the first Saturday in May which 
traditionally marked the start of the 
season in Puget Sound.  See the complete 
press release from WDFW, . Click here
Shrimping Rules Click here.
Good news, the recreational spot 
shrimp season was announced more 
than three months in advance.  
In the next three Newsletters I will 
include spot shrimp advice and tips that 
will get your 80 spot shrimp limit a 
certainty.
First of all, here is a list of the items you 
need for a successful spot shrimp 
harvest.  Before I get started let me give 
you the best tip possible: If you are going 
to cut corners on rigging your spot shrimp 
gear, don't go.  If you try to cut corners 
one of two things are likely to happen: 
1) You will lose your gear 
2) You will not do very well (not fun)
Rigging your shrimp pot correctly is a 
good idea since losing your gear can 
become very expensive.
I rig my shrimp pots with the anticipation 
that I will not lose my pots.  Shrimp pots 
should weigh at least 30 pounds.  There 
are two reasons for 30-pound shrimp 
pots: 
1) The pots are more effective when they 
are stable and do not move because of 
the rope tugging on the shrimp pot. 
2) Once a shrimp pot weighs 30 pounds it 
is unlikely the pot will float away.
Many novice spot shrimp fanatics want to 
cut corners by not purchasing enough 
floatation.  Remember, a completely 
rigged shrimp pot costs between $225 
and $300.  The floats attached to the end 
of the 400 feet of rope are the only life 
line to the shrimp pot. Have enough 
flotation so it will float the shrimp pot in 
the event the pot breaks loose from the 
bottom.  The pot floating away can be 
caused by two events:
1) The current moves the pot
2) Someone gets tangled in your gear. 
They untangle the mess and drag your 
pot into deep water
Without sufficient floatation, the result 
of a tangle with someone else's line is 
usually not good.
Spot Shrimp Gear
˜SMI Shrimp pots round (19001) or 
octagon (19027)
˜400 feet of leaded rope either 1/4" or 
5/16”
˜Heavy duty pot harness
˜Shrimp pot weights
˜Molded buoy
˜Inflatable buoy
˜9” Bait barrel
 
Click here to see shrimp pot gear
Those are the basic items you need for 
rigging a spot shrimp pot.  From there the 
pot can be accessorized to make the pot 
easier to handle and store when the 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
shrimping day has ended.  Click here to 
see rigging a shrimp pot.

This is the time of year to contribute to 
two great events: The Jennings Park 
Kids Fishing Derby and the Everett

dollar that you contribute to either 
event. 
I have been involved in the Blind 
Derby for many years.  The Blind 
people who are involved in this derby 
will pull at your heart strings.  They are 
so full of enthusiasm and excitement.  
Can you only imagine what it is like to 
be on the water salmon fishing and

Englefield 
Bay/Queen 
Charlottes Island
June 19-22
You are invited
There are only a couple spots left to 
fish with Tom Nelson and John 
Martinis at the West Coast Resorts 
Englefield Bay Lodge on Queen 
Charlotte Island, British Columbia. 
Last year I experienced some of the 
best Chinook salmon fishing at 
Englefield Bay ever!  
This is what I enjoyed about the trip; I 
could fish as many hours as I wanted.  
The boats were cleaned each day.  
Bait, tackle and lunch were ready and 
in the boat by the time I got there.  
There were hot lunches brought to 
the fishing area each day.  There was 
no need to go back to the lodge for 
supplies or drop off fish caught in the 
morning.  The same crew that brought 
lunch out also picked up and tagged 
the fish then took them back to the 
lodge to be cleaned and vacuumed 
packed.  This is a well-orchestrated 
lodge.  You get everything they 
promised you and more.
The best way I could describe the 
success of the 2015 fishing trip to 
Englefield Bay is this: Our group of 30 
anglers brought back nearly 3000lbs 
of filled Salmon, Halibut, Ling Cod and 
Rock Fish.  Each angler had two 50lb 
boxes of fish fillets.

Marine Area 9 
Poised to Open for 
Chinook January 16
Area 9 will most likely be open as 
planned on January 16, as per the Sport 
Fishing Rule Book. If so, and I am 
confident it will, Chinook fishing might 
be a modest success. So let's plan on an 
opening.
Since Area 9 and 10 have been closed 
for such a long time, there are some 
things going in our favor when Area 9 
opens.  I believe, due to the closure and 
the absence of fishing, there should be a 
good population of legal sized Chinook 
moving about that have not seen a 
plastic squid or spoon.  Also, it appears 
from the lack of fishing, a larger pool of 
Chinook should be here in January.  It's 
like putting money in the bank and not 
making a withdrawal over time.  Now is 
the payback for waiting to catch a 
Chinook out of Area 9.  Remember Area 
9 and 10 have been closed now for 
about 76 days. This is like closing half of 
Puget Sound to Chinook fishing.   
Here is what I think will be found when 
Area 9 opens: fishing should be 
excellent on Possession Bar, Pilot Point 
and Useless Bay.  Most likely Possession 
Bar will have the best Chinook fishing.  
Because of the near floods we had this 
winter, Mid Channel Bank at Port 
Townsend will probably be where the 
bait and salmon end up.  We shall see. 
When/if the Area 9 Chinook fishing 
starts on January 16, I would bet on

Possession Bar on any days when the 
tide is coming in before noon time.  
On the days that the tide is ebbing 
before noon, I would fish the west 
side of Possession Bar or Mid Channel 
Bank.  As we get closer to the end of 
January and beyond, I would try to 
make it to Mid Channel Bank as often 
as possible.  
Because Areas 8-1 and 8-2 remained 
open during the Area 9 closure, those 
two Areas sharpened our appetite 
while we waited for the main event to 
happen on January 16.  There were 
some sporadic bursts of decent 
Chinook fishing between Hat Island 
and Camano Island. However, that 
Area just does not have the look and 
feel of Area 9.  When Area 9 opens 
there will be twice as many trailers 
parked at the Everett 10th Street Boat 
Launch.

Area 10 Check WDFW
I want to look at some particular spots 
in Area 9 such as Possession Bar and 
Pilot Point.  Most anglers fish for 
Chinook in these Areas without 
understanding the tide effects and 
where fish are located.  No matter 
how I lay it out, there is a good chance 
fish might be located differently from 
m y  r e c o m m e n d a t i o n s .   M y 
recommendations are only good 
starting points for effective Chinook 
fishing. 
Possession Bar is made up of 
several sub fishing areas
1. West side of the bar near the 
Scatchet Head Buoy, sometimes 
called the inner Bar 
2. West side of the bar southeast 
corner 
3. Tin Shed Drift, very southern end 
of the Bar 
4. East side of the Bar southeast 
corner 
5. East side of the Bar near the 
Possession Point Buoy
When heading out, there are a lot of 
places to put your line in the water at 
Possession Bar.  How do you make a 
smart decision?  Unless I have a hot 
fishing report to go by, these are a 
series of choices I would make. I 
always make a stop at the southeast 
corner of Possession Bar and look for 
bait near the bottom in 90 to 120 feet 
o f  w a t e r.   I f  t h e r e  a r e  g o o d 
concentrations of bait, I stay and fish.  
If there is little bait, I move on.  A short 
distance away is the Tin Shed Drift 
(very southern end of the Bar).  It is 
the same routine, look for bait on the 
southern end of the Bar and perhaps 
troll over or closer to the southwest 
corner of the Bar.  Again this is a 
simple routine. Look for bait and try to 
stay in the same area as the bait.  
Most of the winter time I do not fish 
near the Scatchet Head Buoy or the 
Possession Point Buoy for Chinook.  
During the January 2014 Chinook 
season, there was almost no bait on 
Possession Bar.  There is no logic for 
that situation except grinding it out 
and hoping for a stray Chinook to 
come by.  
While fishing Possession Bar for 
Chinook, try to stay in 90 to 120 feet of 
water but not deeper than 150 feet.  
The edges of Possession Bar are quite 
steep, and it is easy to get out of the 
strike zone and easily wander off into 
deep water.
Pilot Point is also made up of sub areas 
for Chinook fishing.  One of the best 
Areas is near the houses on the Beach 
at Pilot Point.  In this area, the bottom 
has some unique contours and sharp 
corners that hold baitfish. When the 
tide is running hard I like to fish from 
the houses on the beach to a quarter 
of the distance to Point no Point.  As 
the tide slows down, I like to fish the 
entire distance from the houses to 
most of the way to Point no Point.  
Don't get too close to Point no Point 
because the water gets weird and 
there will be a ton of seaweed waiting 
for you.  I didn't follow my own advice 
this summer while fishing for Chinook 
and got into that seaweed mess close 
to Point no Point.  Once again, look for 
bait and when you find bait don't 
move too far.  
The bottom at Pilot Point is a more 
graduated contour compared to 
Possession Bar.  You still have to be 
careful to not wander around too 
much.  Try concentrating in 90 to 150 
feet of water at Pilot Point.  Looking 
for bait and sticking with the bait is 
the key issue for tracking down 
Chinook.

Bahia la Tortuga 
Fishing Lodge
One of my many fishing adventures in 
2015 was to Bahia la Tortuga (Bay of 
t h e  T u r t l e )  F i s h i n g  L o d g e 
approximately 100 miles south of 
Zihautenejo/Ixtapa Mexico. I went to 
this Mexican fishing lodge because of 
its remoteness and what I describe as 
an “off the grid” fishing adventure.  
This trip was definitely not roughing it. 
However, the lodge was without hot 
water, TV, internet connection or cell 
phone service for most phones, not 
even windows!  Before you paint a 
picture in your mind of “What the…?”, 
this place is one of the two greatest 
fishing lodges that I have ever fished.  
Bahia la Tortuga Fishing Lodge is the 
neatest most well-manicured fishing 
lodge in all of Mexico.  This place is a 
gem of a find!  John Lorenzo and his 
wife Angie run the lodge.  John is in 
charge of coordinating the fishing and 
Angie runs the kitchen.  I hope that 
you can handle five meals and snacks 
each and every day.
The trip starts at the airport in 
Zihautenejo, Mexico.  Salvador was 
waiting to pick up Anne and me and 
take us to the lodge, a two-hour drive 
through a very scenic and rural part of 
Mexico.  If you have been to Cabo San 
Lucas, Puerto Vallarta or any of the 
other popular tourist destinations in 
Mexico, get ready for a cultural 
immersion in rural southern Mexico.  
Salvador made many stops along the 
way for pictures, purchasing locally 
grown bananas for us and showing us 
where his mother and father are 
buried.
The destination we were headed to 
was Puerto Vicente.  This is a very 
small fishing village in the middle of 
nowhere on the Pacific Ocean.  When 
you arrive, you are in the middle of a 
different era in Mexico.  It is very 
much like what it would have been 
150 years ago, minus the outboard 
motors.  This place is authentic and 
real!  I felt privileged to be associated 
with these people for the short time 
we were there.   Chickens and dogs 
were running loose everywhere.  Pigs 
were in a front yard and a huge soccer 
field was at the marina.  Small mom 
and pop stores dot the landscape.  It is 
a village where everyone knows 
everyone.  John Lorenzo and his wife 
settled here 19 years ago, moving 
from Texas to Mexico.  They settled 
here to live and eventually turned 
their residence into a fishing lodge.  
This is a lodge where people from all 
over the world come to fish.  When I 
was there, there were anglers from 
England, Alberta Canada, Wenatchee 
and us from Mukilteo.  The reason 
people come to the Bahia la Tortuga 
fishing Lodge is because culturally and 
fishing, this is the real deal.  The 
angling was outstanding and “Oh ya” 
with the most stunning silky sand and 
remote beaches in the world, 
Do you want to fish inshore for Bonita 
and Sierra Mackerel or do you want to 
go off shore for Sailfish and Dorado 
(Mahi Mahi)?  On a bad day of fishing, 
you might hook and land 2 to 4 Sailfish 
and Dorado.  On a good day you might 
land 4 to 8 Sailfish.
On the first day, I hooked five Sailfish 
and landed four (all released).  In 
addition, I caught a Dorado that was a 
little over 20 pounds that we kept for 
dinner.  I could have hooked and 
landed a lot more Sails, but quit 
fishing at 11:30 AM because I 
accomplished my goal.  I didn't go to 
see how many Billfish I could hook and 
land.  Anne and I went there to 
immerse ourselves in the laid back life 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
style and culture of a small fishing 
village.  
The day at the lodge starts like this: 
wake-up is at 5:15 AM (if you want) 
and breakfast is at 5:30 AM.  You can 
go fishing at 10 AM if you want to.  At 6 
AM the driver picks you up and takes 
you to the marina only five minutes 
away. The fishing guides are prompt 
and ready to go within minutes of 
your arrival at the marina.  These 
guides are ready to get you out to the 
fishing grounds the minute you step 
into the boat.  The morning is not 
wasted getting bait and making other 
unnecessary stops.  This is all handled 
before you get to the boat in the 
morning. 
Many of the anglers that I met at the 
lodge brought their own fishing 
tackle. If you want to do some light 
line fishing, it would be best to bring a 
fishing rod and reel rated for up to 30 
pounds.  The tackle the guides had 
was good quality; Shimano rods and 
reels.  The reels were filled with 
relatively new line.  The rods supplied 
by the guides were probably rated 30 
to 80 pounds. If you choose to do 
some inshore fishing, then bring a 7 ½ 
foot rod rated for 12 to 20 pounds and 
a 4000 sized spinning reel filled with 
30-pound braid.
If you are planning a warm water 
fishing trip in the near future, I would 
definitely recommend the Bahia La 
Tortuga fishing Lodge.  This is really a 
different experience from fishing out 
of Cabo San Lucas.  Picture this: Great 
fishing, great food, personal service 
and no beach vendors! Click here for 
more information.
Englefield 
Bay/Queen 
Charlottes Island
June 19-22
You are invited
There are only seven spots left to fish 
with Tom Nelson and John Martinis at 
the West Coast Resorts Englefield Bay 
Lodge on Queen Charlotte Island, 
B r i t i s h  C o l u m b i a .  L a s t  y e a r  I 
experienced some of the best Chinook 
salmon fishing at Englefield Bay ever!  
This is what I enjoyed about the trip; I 
could fish as many hours as I wanted.  
The boats were cleaned each day.  
Bait, tackle and lunch were ready and 
in the boat by the time I got there.  
There were hot lunches brought to 
the fishing area each day.  There was 
no need to go back to the lodge for 
supplies or drop off fish caught in the 
morning.  The same crew that brought 
lunch out also picked up and tagged 
the fish then took them back to the 
lodge to be cleaned and vacuumed 
packed.  This is a well-orchestrated 
lodge.  You get everything they 
promised you and more.
The best way I could describe the 
success of the 2015 fishing trip to 
Englefield Bay is this: Our group of 30 
anglers brought back nearly 3000lbs 
of filled Salmon, Halibut, Ling Cod and 
Rock Fish.  Each angler had two 50lb 
boxes of fish fillets.
Included in the package:
Hotel accommodation in Vancouver 
on June 18

to the airport on June 19

to Sandspit via chartered jet

Englefield Bay Lodge
Deluxe accommodations based on 
double occupancy
All chef-prepared meals, snacks and 
soft beverages
Unlimited fishing 
Trips including 5 hours per day of 
guided fishing
Fully equipped 18-foot center console 
boats, 90 hp Mercury outboards, GPS, 
VHF radios and electric down riggers

floatation collar

freezing and boxing of your catch
If you are considering a trip, make 
reservations now.  If you need more 
information, stop by John's Sporting

Smoke Salmon 
Jerky
Needed: Smokehouse and 
food Dehydrator 
Ingredients for 10lbs of 
Salmon
Brown Sugar
Kosher Rock Salt
Kikkoman Teriyaki Sauce
McCormick Montreal Steak 
Seasoning
Honey 
Black Pepper 
Bring four cups of water to a near boil.  
Slowly pour and stir two cups of 
honey into the hot water.
Mix four cups of water, two Cups of 
brown sugar, two cups of kosher salt, 
two cups of Kikkoman Teriyaki Sauce, 
fo u r  t a b l e s p o o n s  M c C o r m i c k 
Montreal Steak Seasoning, four 
tablespoons of black pepper and two 
tablespoons of garlic salt.  Stir until all 
the salt is dissolved. 
Add the dissolved honey and other 
ingredients together into a food grade 
plastic bucket.  Stir until everything is 
well mixed together. 
Slice the Chinook into ¼" slices while 
still half frozen with an electric meat 
slicer. If you do not have a meat slicer 
thaw the salmon and cut with a sharp 
knife.
Put the pieces of salmon into the 
brine and stir to get good coverage.  
Add cold water as needed.  Leave the 
fish in the brine for 24 hours.
Pour the fish into a large colander to 
drain the brine off of the fish. Do not 
wash the fish off with water.
Pour the salmon back into an empty 
brine bucket.  Pour as much Kikkoman 
Teriyaki sauce over the fish so that the 
Teriyaki sauce covers the salmon.  
Leave the salmon in the Teriyaki sauce 
for eight hours.
Now pour the salmon into a colander 
to drain off the Teriyaki sauce.  Do not 
wash the salmon. 
Lay the salmon pieces to dry for 8-12 
hours on a table that is covered with 
foil.  I do this in the garage where it is 
cool.
Bring your smokehouse up to 150 
degrees.  I use a Bradley Smoker and I 
use alder pucks.  Lay the salmon on 
the smokehouse trays and smoke for 
two hours.  Rotate the trays after one 
hour.
Take the trays out of the smokehouse 
after two hour hours. 
Bring the temperature of your 
dehydrator up to 145 degrees prior to.   
placing the salmon on the dehydrator 
trays. Leave the salmon in the 
dehydrator for 1 ½ hours. Take the 
salmon out and vacuum pack or eat 
fresh.

July 1
Here We Go!
Fishing 
Opportunities Galore
As much as we all dislike the closures, 
there have been plenty of opportunities 
to harvest fish and shellfish since 
January 1st.  This is what my year looked 
like so far: fished winter Blackmouth 
until it closed; went razor clam digging 
until it closed; caught Ling Cod at 
Possession Bar and in Area 7; harvested 
Spot Prawns in Area 8-2; caught Coon 
Stripe and Pink Shrimp in Area 8-1 and 
then trapped Spot Shrimp in Area 6 on 
Eastern Bank. Washington State offers 
an incredible amount of opportunities; 
you just have to explore new ideas 
when some of your favorite fishing 
areas are closed.
Starting July 1, again we can get back to 
the fishing areas we all enjoy.  Let me do 
a quick limited run-down of the July 
seasons.
July 1: Area 6  should remain open for 
Spot Shrimp with the limit now set at 
160
July 1: Area 7 opens Chinook fishing for 
hatchery only
July 1: Area 7 West should remain open 
for Spot Shrimp where the limit is now 
160
July 1: Dungeness Crab  opens in most 
areas of Puget Sound
July 1: Tulalip Bubble  (opened 
previously) is open Friday until Monday 
at noon for hatchery Chinook
July 1: Area 9  opens for catch and 
release salmon fishing
July 15: Area 7 South  opens for 
Dungeness Crab
July 16: Area 9  opens for Hatchery 
Chinook
July 16: Area 10  opens for Hatchery 
Chinook
August 1: Area 7 opens for Hatchery or 
Wild Chinook
Marine Area 7 Chinook
If you are planning on fishing the San 
Juan Islands for Chinook, the vast 
majority of the Chinook around the 
perimeter of the Islands are headed to 
the Fraser River in Canada.  Guess 
what?  The Canadians don't mark their 
hatchery Chinook.  That's OK because 
the Chinook fishing will still be decent 
throughout Rosario Strait.  In fact, the 
first two weeks of the season almost 
always provides good Chinook fishing at 
Eagle Bluff, Thatcher Pass, Lopez Flats 
and Point Lawrence. On August 1, all 
Chinook may be retained, hatchery or 
wild.  The popular Chinook fishery at 
Eagle Point on the west-side of San Juan 
Island should just be heating up on 
August 1.  Last year when I was fishing at 
Eagle Point, I caught most of my 
Chinook using a flasher with an 
Anchovy. 
Marine Area 6 Spot Shrimp
If you have not experienced shrimping 
on the SE corner of Eastern Bank, you 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
have been missing an incredible 
opportunity.  Anne and I went 
shrimping on Eastern Bank toward the 
end of June and easily caught our limit 
of 320 Spot Shrimp.  Not only were 
the shrimp easy to catch, the size of 
the shrimp were enormous!  The map 
of the good shrimp area is in my book, 
“Saltwater Fishing Journal”.  If you are 
going, plan on shrimping one to two 
hours before high tide.  If the tides are 
small, you can start shrimping two 
hours before high tide.  If there is a lot 
of water movement don't put your 
pots in the water until an hour before 
high tide.  
Marine Area 7 West Spot 
Shrimp
Area 7 West is also part of the 
expanded Spot Shrimp limit of 160 
shrimp per person.  Near Friday 
Harbor the shrimping is quite good at 
Park Bay and Point Caution.  A bit 
further to the Northwest, good 
shrimping can be had on the west-side 
of Waldron Island.   The tides will 
dictate when you can effectively 
shrimp in all of 7 West.  Plan on 
putting your shrimp pots out one hour 
b efo re h igh  tid e fo r th e b est 
shrimping.
Puget Sound Crab opens July 1
Everyone has their own favorite place 
t o  c a t c h  D u n g e n e s s  C r a b .  
Fortunately, these critters are broadly 
dispersed throughout Puget Sound.  If 
you want easy crabbing: launch your 
boat at the Everett Boat launch, go 
down the river and put your crab pots 
out in front of the Everett Jetty.   This 
is as good as it gets and you will 
probably only burn two gallons of fuel 
by the time you get back to the dock 
with a limit of crab.
If you live on or near Camano Island, 
launch at the State Park on Camano 
and head over to Baby Island or 
Langley to get a limit of crab.
In the Edmonds/Shilshole area, the 
big bay near Richmond Beach is full of 
crab.  A little further to the north of 
Edmonds I would recommend the 
very north end of Browns Bay for 
Dungeness and Red Rock Crab.
A good starting depth for crab would 
be 50 to 60 feet deep.  If two of you 
are putting out four pots, I would start 
the first set like this: One pot at 50, the 
next at 60, the next at 80 and the last 
one at 125 feet deep.  After pulling 
the first set of pots, reconfigure all of 
them to the depth you found to be the 
most productive.  
Crab Bait:  Chicken (fried or raw), 
turkey, salmon, canned mackerel and 
canned Pink salmon are all excellent 
baits for Dungeness Crab.  This is how 
I prepare my bait: I use one SMI bait 
box for fish parts or chicken.  I use one 
SMI 9” bait tube with bait that is 
frozen solid.  My frozen bait consists 
of canned Mackerel, shrimp heads 
that I saved or canned Pink salmon.  I 
t a ke  a n y  o n e  o r  a l l  o f  t h e s e 
ingredients and blend them in a food 
processor.  Once liquefied I pour in 
oatmeal to thicken the mixture up and 
to absorb the scent.  I put the mixture 
in a SMI 9” bait barrel and freeze it for 
a couple of days to make it rock hard.  I 
take the bait barrels out of the freezer 
the morning that I am going crabbing.  
Raw meat/fish and the frozen 
concoction is a deadly mixture for 
catching Dungeness Crab.  
Crab Pots: If you want inexpensive, 
the SMI Square folding pot #19019 is 
about as good as it gets in the folding 
pots.  This particular crab pot has a 
top loading hatch that makes access 
to the crab much easier than similar 
brands.  John's Sporting Goods has 
this pot on sale for $14.95.  John's 
sells complete crab pot kits for $39.95 
and includes the pot, crab measure, 
bait bag, harness and  100 feet of 
leaded rope.
If you want a deluxe setup, the SMI 
Octagon/Round #19037/19035 crab 
pot is the best crab pot money can 
buy.  John's runs either of these pots 
on sale for $79.  Both have 10-inch-
wide doors that make it easy for large 
crab to enter.  Both pots also have a 
built in bait container that is much 
easier to use than a separate bait box.
Marine Area 10 Catch and 
Release Chinook Now Open
I will let you in on a little secret.  Area 
10 near Kingston/Apple Tree Point has 
been red hot for catch and release 
Chinook fishing.  Get on over to the 
south side of Apple Tree Point and 
improve on your Chinook catching 
skills.  Fish with the standard Gibbs 
Red Racer flasher followed by a 
Kingfisher #964 3.5 spoon.  Rig the 
spoon 42 inches behind the flasher 
and tie it together with 30-pound 
leader material. 
Area 8-2 Tulalip Bubble (only) 
Chinook Fishing is now Open
Until July 16, the Tulalip Bubble is the 
only place in the North end of Puget 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
Sound that is open for keeping 
Chinook.  The Bubble is open every 
week Friday, Saturday, Sunday and 
until noon on Monday.  You can also 
fish with two rods if you have the two 
rod endorsement on your fishing 
license.  The best fishing at the Bubble 
is the first hour of the day and the last 
hour of the evening.  I would 
recommend a Gibbs Red Racer flasher 
followed by Goldstar OG142R 
Green/Glow squid 42 inches behind 
the flasher.  You can keep two 
hatchery Chinook.
Marine Area 9 Opens July 16 
for keeping hatchery Chinook
This is the granddaddy of Puget Sound 
recreational fishing.  All of us wait all 
year for this much anticipated season.  
This Chinook season will last from 12 
to 15 days depending on how good 
the fishing goes.  Let's go fishing!
Last year on opening day, I fished at 
Mid Channel Bank with more than 
100 other boats.  Yes, it was very 
crowded but the fishing was still very 
good.  If you don't like crowds, don't 
go near this place. Normally I would 
fish in 90 to 100 feet of water at Mid 
Channel, but on opening day last year 
I fished in 60 feet of water and I did 
quite well and it was a big stress 
reliever being away from the crowds 
out in the deeper water.  I have two 
rigs I prefer for Mid Channel: Gibbs 
Red Racer flasher with a 3.5 #964 
Kingfisher Spoon or a Gibbs Red Racer 
flasher with a Cookies N Cream Coho 
Killer spoon.  Tie either rig together 
with 30-pound leader material and 
make the leader 42 inches in length.  
The best time to fish Mid Channel 
Bank is when the tide is going out.
Depending on tides, this is my 
strategy for fishing Puget Sound 
Chinook.  I fish at Pilot Point when the 
tide is coming in.  If I don't get fish at 
Pilot Point on the incoming tide, I will 
run to Mid Channel and fish the ebb 
tide.  I will do the same thing in 
reverse if the first tide of the day is the 
ebb tide.  In this case, I go to Mid 
Channel first and fish all the way to the 
end of the ebb tide and then head to 
Pilot Point to finish up the day.
Recommend Chinook Tackle
Gibbs Red Racer Flasher
Kingfisher Spoon 3.5 #964
Kingfisher 3.5 #395
Kingfisher 3.5 #675
Pline 30lb Flourocarbon Leader
Sampo X3CB Snap Swivel
Recommended Crab Gear

SMI Hea
vy Duty Harness

Hanford Reach Open for 
Sockeye Fishing
Actions: Opens sockeye salmon to 
retention
Effective date: June 28 through Aug. 
15, 2016
Species affected: Sockeye salmon
Area 1: Columbia River from Hwy. 395 
Bridge at Pasco to the Interstate 182 
Bridge at Richland near Columbia 
Point (CRC 534)
Daily Limit: Daily limit of three (3) 
salmon, of which one (1) may be an 
adult hatchery chinook and two (2) 
may be sockeye. Release wild adult 
chinook.
Area 2: Columbia River from the 
Interstate 182 Bridge to Priest Rapids 
Dam (CRC 535, 536)
Daily Limit: Daily limit of six (6) 
salmon, of which two (2) may be adult 
hatchery chinook and three (3) may 
be sockeye. Release wild adult 
chinook.
Other information: Anglers must use 
barbless hooks when fishing for 
salmon and must have a current 
Washington fishing license, as well as 
a Columbia River Salmon and 
Steelhead Endorsement (CRSSE). 
Anglers may fish with two poles with 
the Two-Pole Endorsement, except 
for sturgeon.
Reason for action: The sockeye run 
has exceeded the pre-season forecast 
of 102,000 fish returning to the river 
mouth (currently ~240,000 at 
Bonneville thru 6/26 with the total 
return now projected to reach 
400,000). Barring extreme high water 
temperatures like 2015 that caused 
u n p re c e d e n t e d  p re - s p a w n i n g 
mortality, sufficient escapement of 
fish to meet spawning needs in the 
Wenatchee and Okanogan Rivers 
should be realized. Over 110,000 
sockeye have crossed McNary Dam, 
and consequently, sockeye retention 
upstream of the Hwy. 395 Bridge at 
Pasco to Priest Rapids Dam can now 
be opened.

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis June 2016
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com
Super Spot Shrimp 
Ideas for June
Just because a major portion of the 
Puget Sound Spot Shrimp season is 
closed it does not mean the season has 
come to an end.  There are still a lot of 
opportunities to harvest Spot Shrimp if 
you are willing to travel to locations still 
open.
Marine Area 6 will most likely be open 
for Spot Shrimp harvesting for a few 
more months.  As a matter of fact, Area 
6 is open every day of the week until 
further notice for Spot Shrimp.
Area 7 West is also open every day of 
the week for harvesting Spot Shrimp. 
Area 7 West shrimp map, Click Here
Statewide shrimp map by area: Click 
Here
Even though Marine Areas 6 and 7 West 
are open every day for Spot Shrimp you 
have to take in account the tide.  If the 
tides are very big it is really not worth 
going shrimping for two reasons: you 
could lose your shrimp pot(s) or you 
might not catch many shrimp.  Take a 
look at a tide book before you decide on 
shrimping in Areas 6 and 7.  The ideal 
days for shrimping are when the tide 
difference is less than six feet.
In both Areas 6 and 7, I found the best 
time to go after Spot Shrimp is an hour 
before high tide until an hour after the 
tide.  Spot shrimp can be caught at all 
stages of the tide in these Areas but it is 
tough pickings when the water is 
moving really fast.
Area 6 Spot Shrimp Maps
Lawson Reef
Eastern Bank
Dallas Bank
Partridge Bank
Area 7 West Spot Shrimp Maps 
Park Bay
Spiden/Stuart Islands
Waldron Island
Rigging Spot Shrimp Pots for 
Areas 6 and 7 
If you go to either of these areas 
without a shrimp pot properly rigged 
you will probably lose your shrimp pot.  
Here are some tips.  The shrimp pot 
must weigh 30 pounds.  Attach a small 
folding anchor with a 10-foot rope to 
the bottom of the trap.  Use a Polyform 
LD2 buoy and two of the regular size 
molded yellow buoys for flotation.  
These buoys will float 50 pounds.  The 
extra buoys will achieve two things: 
They will float the shrimp pot and rope if 
the pot floats into deeper water and 
they will prevent the rope from 
dragging the buoys underwater when 
the tide is moving.   
I would not put any extra weight in the 
shrimp pot making it weigh more than 
30 pounds because it will make the Ace 
Line Hauler or Scotty pot puller slow 
down.  A typical shrimp pot weighs 30 
pounds; has 10 to 12 pounds of leaded 
rope attached; a harness weighing a

more of bait in the pot.  This makes 
the whole outfit weigh close to 50 
pounds.
Shrimp Bait additive 
The last day Puget Sound was open for 
Spot Shrimp, I tried a new addition to 
the bait.  I used the normal Spot 
Shrimp bait formula that most of you 
have seen on the Shrimp Pot Rigging 
handout at John's Sporting Goods. 
Click here for shrimp pot rigging and 
bait formula .  In a food processor I 
mixed Icy Point Pink Canned Pink 
Salmon with Mackerel until it was 
almost a liquid. I added some oatmeal 
to make the slurry thicker.  I poured 
the contents into a 6-inch bait barrel 
until the barrel was 7/8 full and froze 
it.  I took the bait barrels out of the 
freezer on the morning I went 
shrimping.  In each of my shrimp pots 
was a 9 inch bait barrel with the 
regular Spot Shrimp Bait and a 6 inch 
bait barrel with the frozen slurry.  This 
seemed to work rather well.  The 
frozen slurry leached out of the bait 
barrel at just the right rate.  By the 
time we were done shrimping at 1PM 
the 6 inch bait barrels were now half 
full.  On that day seven of us caught 
560 Spot Shrimp.
I purchased the Icy Point canned Pink 
Salmon at Bartells when they ran it on 
sale for $1.99 a can. 
Puget Sound 
Ling Cod
Puget Sound Ling Cod is still open until 
June 15.  The crowds have really died 
down out on Possession Bar and now 
it is time to give it another try.
Time to Try 
Something Different
Sole/Flounder
There are many anglers who just want 
to go out on the Sound and catch 
anything that bites.  I realize not all of 
us are “gung-ho” salmon, Ling Cod or 
Halibut anglers.  There are many 
anglers who just want to free 
themselves from downriggers, 
flashers and all the complicated gear 
and regulations associated with 
catching some of these fish species.  If 
you fit the mold, I have the perfect 
thing for you and you will catch loads 
of fish.
Everywhere else south of us on the 
Pacific Coast catching Rock Sole, Sand 
Dabs and English Sole is a big deal.  
Let's call these sole “flounder” for lack 
of a better description. There is close 
to twenty species of sole/flounder in 
Puget Sound.  Most of these fish look 
so identical to one another that you 
can't tell the difference.  The one 
thing they do have in common is their 
great quantity.  When I say great 
quantity, I mean there are loads of 
flounder in Puget Sound.  Some areas 
o f  t h e  S o u n d  h a v e  g r e a t e r 
populations than others.  There are 
some places which have the small 
Sand Dabs and other places which 
have flounder which are dinner plate 
size.
Rock Sole, Sand Dabs and English Sole 
are easy to catch without any 
complicated fishing gear.  This is what 
you need: Gamakatsu Top and Bottom 
Fish Rig #238109.  This is a two hook 
rig with a swivel on both ends of the 
rig.  One swivel attaches to the fishing 
line and the other attaches to a 
weight.  Attach a 4 ounce weight to 
the end of the rig.
The best bait to use is squid.  Although 
flounder will bite on nearly anything, 
a small piece of squid will stay on 
better than most other baits.
Drop this rig to the bottom and hold 
the rod still until a flounder bites the 
hook.  Adjust the line with the 
changing bottom depth as you drift 
along.  This time of year flounder will 
be in 65 to 75 feet of water.
The best spot to catch flounder is 
slightly east of the Langley Marina. 
Click Here for Map.  I fished this spot 
three weeks ago for flounder and 
caught flounder every time I let my 
line to the bottom.  Many times I 
caught two flounder at once.  There 
are so many flounder in this area it will 
take only a few seconds to get a fish on 
the end of the line.  When I say “a few 
seconds”, I mean it happens the 
moment the rig gets near the bottom.
If you want larger flounder but fewer 
of them, head to Mutiny Bay on the 
south side of Whidbey Island.  
Flounder can be found in Mutiny Bay 
in 75 to 100 feet of water.  The 
flounder here are dinner plate size.
Another place to catch good sized 
flounder is on Possession Bar in 35 to 
45 feet of water.
The limit on sole is 15 fish per person.  
If there are two of you fishing, you will

Remember, the barbless hook rule is 
also in effect for these fish.
Cleaning flounder: cut around the 
perimeter of the fish and then pull the 
brown skin off with a pliers.  Leave the 
white skin on the fish.  Cut the gut, 
head and tail off of the fish.
Frying flounder: Coat the fish with 
your favorite fish coating and fry 
them.  The white skin easily pulls off 
the fish after it is fried.
