Things to Consider
Lake Roosevelt:  Huge Kokanee and 
Rainbow trout are being caught.
Lake Stevens: Good kokanee fishing 
will last through June.
Lake Chelan: Kokanee and Mackinaw 
will be quite good through June.
Icicle River:  near Leavenworth will 
open Monday (May 16) until further 
notice for hatchery-marked spring 
chinook fishing.
Kelp Greenling: A very under looked 
and under-fished fish that are 
extremely good eating.  These fish are 
readily available around all kelp beds 
in Area 7.
Lower Columbia Spring Chinook: 
Anglers fishing the lower Columbia 
River can catch and keep spring 
chinook salmon for four more days in 
May – including Memorial Day 
weekend – and up to 13 days in June 
under an agreement reached today by 
fishery managers from Washington 
and Oregon. Click Here for full story
Everett Steelhead & Salmon Club Presents: 
King and Sockeye Salmon   
Opportunities on the Upper 
Columbia River 
by Mark Gavin who is a Longtime PSA member 
 and Salmon University Staffer 
 
Mark will cover 3 outstanding fisheries!  The Summer Sockeye fishery, the 
Summer King (aka “June Hogs”) fishery and the world famous Fall King 
fishery (aka Upriver Brights).  He will provide details on run timing, the best 
places to fish, proven tactics plus some guide secrets to improve your 
success!   This year’s Fall King return is predicted to be the third largest 
ever!  He will tell how to target these fish and even enjoy 2 of the most 
friendly salmon derbies in the PNW.  They are Atomic Salmon Derby and 
the “King of the Reach” Live Capture Brood Stock Derby.

My popular Chinook seminar will be 
held on March 16.  Mike Greenleaf and I 
will be presenting winning strategies 
guaranteed to put more Chinook in your 
boat. We will talk about correct 
methods to rig flashers and spoons as 
well as fishing with herring.  In addition, 
we will go over some fishing charts that 
should help getting to the correct 
fishing spot on the right tide.  Take the

The Everett Steelhead and Salmon Club

$250. Tickets for the derby are $100 
per boat and that includes up to four 
anglers per boat.
The weather last year was absolutely 
brutal during the Everett Blackmouth 
Derby.  The wind blew 20 to 30 mph. 
With that kind of weather, you would 
have assumed an angler with a 
medium to small boat never stood a 
chance of winning the Derby.  Dale 
Helgesson, who won the $3000 first 
prize, tucked behind the north side of 
Hat Island in 60 feet of water to get 
out of the wind.  Dale put out a 
herring and came up with a 16.12-
pound Chinook to win the Derby.  You 
don't need to go far or have a large 
boat in order to get a decent chance at 
winning the Everett Blackmouth 
Derby.  Purchase your ticket right now 
at John Sporting Goods, because if 
you wait to the last minute, “you'll be 
sorry”.
Next, let's explore some winning 
strategies for putting that winning 
Chinook in the boat on March 19.  In 
the last few weeks most of the larger 
Chinook have been caught in front of 
Camano Island State Park and 
Onamac Point on the northwest side 
of Camano Island.  Also, I might state 
that Chinook fishing in either of the 
t w o  a r e a s  h a s  b e e n  a t  b e s t 
inconsistent. 
The southern end of Green Bank near 
Baby Island has been holding a 
considerable amount of bait and a few 
legal size Chinook.  
Another area occasionally putting out 
Chinook in the mid to low teens has 
been the bar running between Hat 
Island and Camano Island, locally 
known as the “racetrack”.
If you want quantities of fish, the most 
southern end of Possession Bar (Tin 
Shed Drift), has been putting out legal 
Chinook that are averaging an inch or 
two over legal size.  That will not win 
any Chinook fishing Derby.  
Pilot Point has also been a consistent 
producer of Chinook that are 
averaging 5 to 7 pounds.  Once again, 
it will be difficult claiming first prize 
with a 5 to 7-pound Chinook.
Point no Point to Skunk Bay has been 
putting out a handful of Chinook 
averaging 5 to 7 pounds.  This area 
holds loads of bait fish.  You would 
think a respectable Chinook in Puget 
Sound would be feeding in this area 
with the quantity of bait available, but 
“it ain't necessarily so”. 
Useless Bay is one of my favorite 
places to fish for Chinook this time of 
year and has been substandard for the 
last 30 days.
Port Townsend's “Mid Channel Bank” 
was loaded with bait fish but salmon 
fishing has not been that good. 
However, I would rate it high on my list 
for putting a $3000 Chinook in my 
boat on tournament day.  The March 
19 Port Townsend low tide is early at 
9:03 AM.  With the tide so early in the 
morning, consider going to Port 
Townsend the day before the Derby so 
you can have ample fishing time.  
The March 19 tides for Inner-Puget 
Sound are: 9:57 AM low tide and 3:04 
PM high tide.
That 9:57 AM low tide rules out two 
areas at daylight on March 19: Pilot 
Point and Useless Bay.  All the other 
areas mentioned can be successfully 
fished until the 9:57 AM low tide.  
After 9:57 AM, the tide starts coming 
in and you can consider fishing Pilot 
Point and Useless Bay. 
With two people fishing, I have been 
fishing whole herring and no flasher 
on one downrigger 100% of the time.  
On the other downrigger I have been 
u s i n g  e i t h e r  o f  t h e s e  t w o 
combinations: Gibbs Red Racer 
Flasher with a #395 Coho Killer 42 
inches behind the flasher or a Gibbs 
Red Racer Flasher with a #964 3.5 
Kingfisher Spoon 42 inches behind the 
flasher. I have been relatively 
successful employing this strategy for 
Chinook this winter. There are times 
when I end up using flashers and 
spoons on both downriggers.  You will 
know when the herring bite goes flat, 
that's when you change.  I never fish 
whole herring on both downriggers.  I 
like to rely on at least one flasher to 
bring the fish into the gear.  Then the 
fish can make up their mind whether 
they want to strike a whole herring or 
a spoon that is an imitation of herring 
or candlefish.  The strategy has been 
working quite well for me this winter.
Tip: when I am using whole herring I 
tie my leaders with 20 pound test and 
3/0 hooks.

Rigging Herring
7 Reasons to fish 
Area 7
The closure of Area 6 for Chinook 
fishing was somewhat depressing. 
Really, I was looking forward to fishing 
Area 6 in March and into April and 
then it closed.   In retrospect, I look at 
the closure as a reason to force myself 
to fish other areas I do not ordinarily 
fish. Lucky me, I have done that with 
an abundance of success.
After the Area 6 closure I focused my 
Chinook fishing on: Salmon Bank near 
Cattle Point (Middle Channel), Hein 
Bank, the northwest side of Eastern 
Bank and McArthur Bank.  Actually, 
this has been a remarkable fishing 
experience.  Not one of the places I 
mentioned will be hitting on all 
cylinders every day. The everyday 
routine is the same: hopscotch 
around until you find a single fish or 
two, then off to the next spot.  It 
seems like a lot of moving around but 
it's actually kind of fun. It's a hunt and 
very rewarding!
If you have been fishing in Area 7 
lately, you know there has been a 
severe lack of bait fish.  This makes 
C h i n o o k  f i s h i n g  a  l i tt l e  m o re 
challenging.  Normally you can find 
bait in any of these areas and then 
work the area really hard.  The fishing 
strategy this year is to fish in one 
direction for maybe a mile or more 
and then worked that same area over 
again.  Most days you will catch at 
least one legal Chinook for every mile 
that you fish.  This doesn't seem like a 
strategy.  I call it, “grinding it out”.  It 
works and the Chinook fishing has 
been reasonably good.  
I wish I could pinpoint some specific 
areas for fishing in Area 7, but I can't.  I 
don't even go to the same place to fish 
on different fishing trips.  I do 
encourage you to fish the areas I 
mentioned because Chinook fishing 
has been a slightly above average and 
on some days extremely good.  
I usually fish one area if I continue to 
see large fish marks on the fishfinder.  
If I fish an hour and have little activity, I 
leave and hit another area.  Don't 
grind it out in one area if you're not 
running into large fish marks. Don't 
assume fishing is done for the day just 
because one area went south.  On one 
particular fishing trip (February 25), 
the best fishing was right in the 
middle of the day.  The tide and time 
of day had no bearing on the bite that 
came on mid-afternoon.  One of my 
good friends and fishing guide, Derek 
Floyd (Reel Class Charter) was fishing 
a totally different area on February 25 
and caught all his fish before noon.  
My point is, these fish are moving 
around from Bank to Bank and you 
need to be willing to do the same until 
you get on top of the them.  
Here are some tips: fish a tad bit 
deeper than normal.  I would 
recommend 125 to 135 feet deep.  
Always start the day fishing one line 
rigged with whole herring and one rod 
rigged with a flasher and spoon.  Use 
the same flashers and spoons I 
recommended in the first part of this 
article.

trouble opening up snaps on the

can honestly say that this is one of the 
best products to hit the fishing tackle 
market in a long time.  This swivel 
allows you to easily change fishing 
rigs.  You can simply rig or un-rig a 
piece of fishing gear no matter how 
cold it is.  This is a must-have item!

Tom Nelson and I have used the Daiwa 
Tanacom 750 in Sitka Alaska and 
Canada for Halibut fishing.  The 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
average depth we fished was 400 feet. 
That's deep if you are hand cranking.  
Not deep at all if you are using the 
Tanacom 750.  Tom and I have 
wrestled Halibut off the bottom with 
ease.  The Tanacom 750 has adequate 
power and a good drag system for any 
size fish in the Pacific Northwest and 
Alaska. This reel holds 440 yards of 65-

change the electrical plug to fit your 
downrigger outlet or you can use the 
battery clamps supplied to attach the 
power cord to your boat battery.  I 
have sold many of these reels and 
have not had one single complaint.

on sale.  When your purchase this reel 
from us, we will fill it with 65 or 80 
pound braided line for free (a $44 
savings).

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis                                       May 2016
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com

The Marysville Kiwanis Club, Everett 
Steelhead and Salmon Club, John's 
Sporting Goods and Marysville Parks, 
Culture and Recreation are sponsoring 
the 22nd Annual free Fishing Derby. 
C h i l d r e n  m a y  b r i n g  t h e i r  o w n

provided. A limit of one fish per entrant 
is enforced. Door prizes and grand

leave pets at home. If you have any

Mark Your Calendar
The three big fishing events for May are: 
the opening of Ling Cod season on May 
1st; Halibut opening on May 7th and 
finally Spot Shrimp opening on May 
14th for the Puget Sound/San Juan area.  
With all the negative news about the 
2016 Puget Sound salmon fishing 
season, there is still plenty of fishing and 
catching to be done without much 
imagination in this region.
Consistently 
Catching Ling Cod
Ling Cod and Halibut are my favorite 
two fish to catch.  I believe many of you 
agree that fresh Ling Cod is the best 
tasting fish to come from the sea.  
The Ling Cod fishing season opening 
every year on May 1st in Puget Sound is 
what gets the ball rolling.  This is the 
time when boats come out of storage 
and we start taking inventory of our 
fishing tackle (if we can find it) left over 
from last year.
You would think that a large body of 
water like Puget Sound would have rock 
piles overflowing with Ling Cod - not so.  
Most of Puget Sound is deep and full of 
glacial mud and sand deposited during 
the last Ice Age.  There are a few natural 
rock or man-made piles in Puget Sound.  
They are scattered throughout the 
Sound and might not be convenient for 
you to get to unless you live near one of 
these areas.
A short list of places for Ling Cod 
fishing in Puget Sound: 
Artificial reef at Hat Island (Gedney 
Island)
Possession Bar
Artificial reef at Possession Bar
Double Bluff
Breakwater around Edmonds Marina
Breakwater around Shilshole Marina
Foul Weather Bluff

through Sunday May 26 - 29.

There are a number of other Ling Cod 
fishing areas throughout the Sound 
that might be a personal favorite.
These are two methods 
for catching Ling Cod: 
live bait 
plastic worms on lead head jigs.
The three primary live baits for 
catching Ling Cod are: Live Rock Sole 
(flounders), Sculpins and small Pile 
Perch (Poggies). Rock Sole can be 
caught just about anywhere in Puget 
Sound that has a sandy bottom.  They 
can be found in 65 to 100 feet of 
water.  These fish are fairly easy to 
catch.  If you mess up catching Rock 
Sole, you need to find another hobby.  
Here is how you rig up for catching 
Sole: slide a Slydo onto the fishing line 
and then tie a #7-barrel swivel onto 
the end of the line.  Tie a short leader 
with a #6 worm hook on 10-pound 
leader material.   The best bait for 
catching Sole is small pieces of squid.  
Even though Sole will bite on anything 
that you send to the bottom, Squid 
will stay on the hook better than most 
other baits since it is so tough.  Once 
you let the bait to the bottom, the 
trick to catching Sole is to hold the 
fishing rod as still as possible.  Don't 
jerk the rod when you start getting a 
bite.  Let the Sole hook himself.  Don't 
be aggressive, these fish will hook 
themselves and the job will get done 
sooner if you can show some 
patience.   For three anglers, you will 
need 12 to 15 flounder for a day of 
fishing.  Keep the Sole alive by placing 
them in an ice chest and pouring five 
gallons of water in the ice chest every 
hour or use an aerator. Sculpins can be 
caught while fishing for Rock Sole and 
are the ultimate Ling Cod bait.  It 
would be nice if they could be caught 
in larger quantities during Ling Cod 
season.
Small Pile Perch can be caught in and 
around most pilings in Puget Sound.  
They are also found in many of the 
marinas here in the Sound.  If 
available, you see them around pilings 
and under the docks.  Pile Perch can 
be caught on herring/smelt jigs.  The 
#4 Gamakatsu Herring jig with fish 
skin (without glow beads) is the best 
jig to use for catching Pile Perch.
The next question is, “how to hook-up 
live bait now that you caught them?”  
Here is one Ling Cod rig I like: tie a 
double hook rig with a 5/0 black 
Gamakatsu Circle hook and a 6/0 
black Gamakatsu Octopus hook.  The 
Circle hook should be the top hook.  
Tie the hooks three inches apart on 
30-pound test leader material.  The 
leader length should be no longer 
than 30 inches.  If you make it longer, 
it will get tangled around the line 
when you are letting the rig to the 
bottom.
Here is the complete rig from the line 
to the leader:  put a large Slydo on the 
fishing line.  Next tie a #5 black barrel 
swivel on the end of the line.  Tie the 
leader to the other end of the swivel.  
Now snap a 4 to 6-ounce cannon ball 
lead to the Slydo.
Gently grab a live bait and insert the 
circle hook through the inside of the 
mouth of the fish and out through the 
top of the head.  Now I am going to 
give you the best tip ever on keeping 
the live fish on the hook.  Once the live 
fish is on the hook, take a Buzz Bomb 
bumper and slide the bumper over 
the tip of the hook until it rests against 
the live bait.  This Buzz Bomb bumper 
will prevent live fish from wiggling off 
the hook and that saves on bait and 
keeps you fishing.
Live Bait Gear List
Slydo Sinker Slide

Now let me give you a practical tip on 
rigging tackle for Ling Cod fishing.  
Ling Cod are called rock fish for one 
simple reason - they live in a very 
rocky environment.  Because of this 
environment it lends itself to being a 
tackle grabber.  If you are going fishing 
all day, bring at least three complete 
rigs per angler.  
Fishing with live bait is not as easy as 
letting the bait to the bottom and 
waiting for a Ling Cod to jump on the 
hooks.  This is a technique that will 
put a limit of Lings in the boat if you 
have patience. When Ling Cod go 
after a live bait they want to eat, they 
do so with some suspicion.  Most 
often they will initially try to stun the 
bait.  If you strike during this phase of 
the bite, you will most likely never 
hook-up a Ling and get him in.  Let the 
Ling get comfortable with the fact that 
the bait is the real deal.  Eventually 
the biting Ling will grab the bait and 
try to take it back to the bottom.  Do 
not strike at this phase of the bite.  
Wait until the Ling is taking line off the 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
reel.  Now start slowly reeling and the 
Ling will get hooked-up.
Ling Fishing with Plastic Baits
Fishing with artificial baits for Ling 
Cod can never go out of style.  They 
are easy to use and can be very 
productive. There are two types of 
plastic baits considered worth 
purchasing for Ling Cod fishing: 6-inch 
Twin Tail Scampi's and Hogy 5 inch 
Flounders.  Twin Tail Scampi come in a 
variety of colors. If I were to pick out a 
couple Scampi Tails colors for Ling 
fishing I would choose motor oil with 
red flake or black with silver flake.  
The Scampi tails need to be paired up 
with 4 or 6-ounce lead head jigs.  
Hogy Flounder can be rigged exactly 
how I earlier described for using a real 
Rock Sole.
The technique for using Scampi Tails 
and Hogy Flounders is to make them 
look like live swimming fish.  In other 
words, don't radically jig the baits 
which is not natural.  There is nothing 
swimming near the bottom that is 
jumping around like a rabbit on 
steroids.  Gently swim the baits so 
that they mimic a live swimming fish.  
The whole trick is to make the artificial 
bait look like a live natural swimming 
bait that could be a potential Ling Cod 
meal.
This is where things become tricky if 
you have not fished for Ling Cod.  A 
Ling Cod will always grab the artificial 
bait on the down-stroke of the rod.  If 
you are waiting for a massive strike, 
give me a call when you are tired of 
fishing.  The trick while jigging is to 
watch the fishing line at all times.  
When a Ling picks up the artificial bait 
the fishing line will go limp, then strike 
hard with your fishing rod and crank 
hard on the reel.  Don't take any 
chances if you remotely think a Ling 
has picked up the bait.

September 2016
Newsletter
The September Newsletter is packed 
with new material.  I have included four 
new maps: Hood Canal Coho, Hood 
Canal Chinook, Open Bay Chinook and 
Kingston Chinook.  With the exception 
of Kingston/Area 10, these new maps 
will guide you to some new areas that 
perhaps you have not fished.  With the 
closures that we have at hand,  it is 
time to expand your universe 
to 
include some of the areas that I have 
outlined in the Newsletter.  Good luck 
fishing!
New Focus on 
Salmon Fishing
None of us enjoy fishing closures that 
happen in our own backyard. Anglers 
who do not  live in the Seattle – 
Edmonds - Everett metropolitan area 
have more open salmon seasons and 
bigger limits on either Chinook or Coho.  
Say what? Increased limits?  That's 
right, now there are increased Chinook 
limits (four Chinook per day) in the 
southern end of Hood Canal.  Also, 
there is a four fish limit on Coho in the 
north end of Hood Canal.  In addition, 
there is a four Coho limit on the (Big) 
Quilcene River which flows into Hood 
Canal near Dabob Bay.  The Cowlitz 
River has been nothing short of 
spectacular for Summer Run Steelhead.  
The Samish River near Bow/Edison is 
open for Chinook, and the fishing has 
been reasonably good.
Marine Area 7 (San Juan's) is open for 
either hatchery or wild Chinook until 
th
September 30 . This is just a handful of 
fishing opportunities within driving 
distance from the Everett/Seattle area.  
In this Newsletter I want to take a close 
look at some of the areas I mentioned 
previously and provide you with some 
new maps.  I am going to make two 
Hood Canal maps (Area 12) and a 
Kingston map (Area 10).  The Kingston 
map is in anticipation of the November

their catch reports on time face a $10

"Catch reports play a major role in 
determining how much crab will be 
available for winter harvest." said Rich 
Childers, WDFW's shellfish policy

reports from everyone licensed to fish 
for crab in Puget Sound - whether or 
not they caught crab this year."
Childers said WDFW will announce 
winter crab seasons for Puget Sound 
in early October after completing the 
assessment of the summer fishery.

Fishing for Chinook at Kingston/Apple Tree Point can take

year the bait will present itself at varying depths.

maps.text:
Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis                                December 2016
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com
Area 9 Closes
Area 7 Opens
Areas 8-1, 8-2, 10 remain open
When Marine Area 9 closes for salmon 
fishing we must look for other windows 
of opportunity. Yes, there are plenty of 
other salmon fishing areas to explore.  
In this Newsletter, I will point out a 
variety of salmon areas which I believe 
are worth taking some time to fish.
Before I get into the heart of the matter, 
I should define what will open starting 
December 1st.  Marine Area 8-1 and 8-2 
will remain open.  Also, on December 
1st, Marine Areas 6, 7 and 10 will open.
The Sport Fishing Rule Book shows a 
Chinook limit of two fish in Marine 
Areas 6 and 7.  The Chinook limit has 
been reduced to one Chinook in Marine 
Areas 6 and 7, much like it was in Areas 
8-1, 8-2, 9 and 10.  To be sure of the 
current salmon fishing regulations for 
the Area that you plan on fishing, go to 
this link and click on the Area you are 
interested in fishing: Click Here
In Marine Areas 8-1 and 8-2 (Saratoga 
Passage Area) there are several good 
salmon spots worth fishing during a 
morning tide.  The beauty of fishing 
Marine Area 8-1 is that most waters in 
the Saratoga Passage are protected 
from harsh southerly winds which 
plague salmon anglers this time of year.  
There is a good boat launch at Camano 
Island State Park which is in the middle 
of some prime salmon fishing areas.  If 
you wish, you can launch at the Park and 
fish for salmon in Elger Bay or right in 
front of the State Park.  This is a perfect 
situation for anglers with smaller boats 
who do not want to venture too far. This 
is also a great salmon fishing area if you 
only have an hour or two to fish because 
you will be five minutes from the boat 
launch at all times.  Because this is close 
to the launch site, you are not making 
compromises for chances to catch 
salmon in a more distant area.
If you want to launch at Camano Island 
State Park and feel you want to go on 
more of an adventure, head to the 
northern end of Camano Island near 
Rocky Point.  Salmon fishing at Rocky 
Point has been quite good this winter 
and it is easy to fish.  You can start 
fishing around Rocky Point and follow 
the bar in 90 feet of water which turns 
into Skagit Bay.
Marine Area 8-2 (Everett Area) can be 
accessed from the 10th Street Boat 
Launch in Everett.  Many good salmon 
fishing areas in Marine Area 8-2 can be 
accessed within fifteen to twenty 
minutes from the boat launch in 
Everett.  
The number one salmon fishing area in 
Area 8-2 which consistently puts out 
decent size Chinook is an area local 
salmon anglers call the “Race Track”.  
The Race Track is simply the bar that 
runs from Hat Island (Gedney Island) to 
Camano Island.  This is a rather narrow 
strip of real estate that runs from one 
island to the other.  The average depth

of this bar is 90 to 120 feet deep.  This 
narrow strip holds large quantities of 
bait in the wintertime which attracts 
and holds Chinook to this area.  The 
Race Track has been a “go to” plan in 
every salmon anglers play book for 
decades.
Marine Area 10 which is open 
November 1st to February 28th, is 
adjacent to Marine Area 9 which 
closes the day before.  So, what's the 
significance of that?  The southern 
border of Area 9 is the northern 
border of Area 10.  All of us who have 
fished in Area 9 in November can 
attest to how good the fishing was.
Here is the plan for Area 10:   When 
the tide is going out I recommend 
fishing from Presidents Point to Jeff 
Head.  I would also work the south 
side of Jeff Head and slightly into Port 
Madison.  When the tide is coming in, 
I would work the south side of the bar 
at Apple Tree Point and into Apple 
Tree Cove.  Most anglers regard this 
the Kingston Area.  Remember this is 
only ten minutes from the outer bar of 
Possession.  This is also a short run 
from the Edmonds Marina and a little 
more travel time from the Shilshole 
Marina or the Everett Marina.  These 
areas are the best spots in Marine 
Area 10.
The areas that I mentioned in Area 10 
should be fished for Chinook in 90 to 
125 feet of water.  These areas have a 
defined edge that you should follow 
with a degree of accuracy.
As a side note: Chinook fishing was 
quite good at Kingston in November.
Chinook Maps for Puget Sound
Elger Bay
Hat Island
Kingston
Many salmon anglers have been 
anxiously waiting for Marine Area 7 to 
open for Chinook on December 1st.  
When Area 7 does open it is anyone's 
guess to where the Chinook will be 
hanging out in good numbers. Rosario 
Straits is the first place that I would 
start exploring for Chinook.
To be effective at Chinook fishing in 
Rosario Strait you must work tides 
which are best for each particular 
location. If you don't have that 
specific information this is what my 
Newsletter is all about - helping you 
become better salmon anglers by 
sorting out all these details.
Here is a list of Chinook fishing places 
in Rosario and the appropriate tides 
to fish those areas: Lopez Flats on the 
East side of Lopez Island (Ebb Tide); 
Reef Point on the south end of 
Cypress Island (Ebb Tide); Eagle Bluff 
on the North End of Cypress Island 
(Flood Tide) and Thatcher Pass on the 
south end of Blakely Island (Ebb Tide). 
As you can see most of the Chinook 
fishing spots in Rosario are best fished 
when the tide is going out.
You will find the best depths to fish for 
wintertime Chinook in the in the San 
Juan's to be an average of about 90 to 
100 feet deep. In most of these areas, 
if you fish out beyond the 100 feet 
depth line there will be too much 
current. Because of all the rocky 
contours which make up the San Juan 
Islands, fish tend to hang close to the 
bottom and at the edges of these 
rocky structures. In most good salmon 
fishing areas, the rocky structure ends 
and the bottom becomes sandy. 
These sandy areas are a perfect 
habitat for Sand Lance and Candlefish 
which is the main food source for 
salmon in the San Juan's.
Another San Juan area I would put at 
the top of my list is Parker Reef on the 
north end of Orcas Island. I like fishing 
Parker Reef on the incoming tide.  
Keep this spot in mind because many 
top Chinook Derby salmon are caught 
from this location.
Chinook Maps for the 
San Juan Islands
Lopez Flats
Thatcher Pass
Eagle Bluff
Parker Reef
Trolling Speeds for 
Winter Chinook 
Fishing
When I recommend trolling at 2.0 to 
2.5 mph for Chinook, I am over-
simplifying effective trolling speeds. 
Downrigger cable angle always has 
precedence over trolling speed. I like 
that classic 45-degree cable angle 
when trolling for Chinook. To keep 
that 45-degree angle, you must 
constantly control boat speed as the 
tide increases or decreases in velocity.
Recently I was fishing at Mid Channel 
Bank at Port Townsend. I only fish Mid 
Channel during the Ebb tide which 
means I am trolling from East to West. 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
The day I was fishing, the tide was 
moving fast enough to make me troll 
3.5 to 4.0 mph.  If I didn't troll that 
speed my downrigger cable would 
have been hanging straight up and 
down.  The point is there are special 
situations when you must troll faster 
than the typical 2.0 to 2.5 mph. Watch 
that cable angle!
How Close 
to the Bottom
Fishing for winter Chinook requires 
you to fish within five feet of the 
bottom.  So how do you know how 
close you are to the bottom with your 
fishing gear?  There is only one 
measurement that works with any 
kind of accuracy.  While at the correct 
trolling speed drop the downrigger 
ball to the bottom and bring the ball 
back about two feet.  A minute later 
let the ball to the bottom again and 
bring it back five feet.  The reason that 
the ball is let out twice in such a short 
time period is so that the ball and 
cable can adjust to the trolling speed.  
Don't worry about getting hung up on 
the bottom with the downrigger ball 
because chances of that happening 
are remote.

I will be having a Chinook Fishing 
Seminar November 4, 2016 at Bayside 
Marine.  The Seminar starts at 7PM.  My 
P o w e r P o i n t  C h i n o o k  f i s h i n g 
presentation will include some very 
useful information on how to become a 
successful salmon angler.  This seminar 
is for the most experienced salmon 
angler as well as the beginner.  If you 
pick up just a single nugget of

TRAVEL EDITION
ENGLEFIELD BAY
The most incredible salmon 
fishing experience ever
If you are like me, you might be planning 
a 2017 salmon, halibut lingcod 
adventure somewhere north of 
Washington State to either Canada or 
Alaska.
This year I fished at Sitka, Alaska and at 
the Queen Charlotte Islands in British 
Columbia.  Both were memorable 
fishing trips.  My trip to Englefield Bay at 
Haida Gwaii on the Queen Charlottes 
Island was the best salmon, lingcod 
halibut fishing trip that I have ever 
experienced.  I thought this adventure 
last year (2015) was outstanding and 
that it could not get any better, but it 
was in 2016.  What a treat and a 
wonderful surprise.  Does this sound 
like something you are interested in 
doing?  If the answer is yes, get your 
deposit in now because most everyone 
who went this year are returning in 
2017.
The first day of the journey to Englefield 
Bay is a drive to Vancouver, BC.  The 
price of the package includes an 
overnight stay at the River Rock Casino 
in Vancouver.  The next morning 
transportation is provided to the 
Airport.  When you envision airports, 
you think of long lines and security 
checks.  None of that happens on this 
trip.  The charter flight from Vancouver

to Sandspit is at a small terminal 
where everything is simple, easy and 
geared toward destination fishing 
travel.  You check your bag and get on 
the plane.  It's that simple!
The charter flight which is included in 
the package price takes you on a 45 
minute flight to Sandspit on Queen 
Charlotte Island.  At Sandspit, there 
are helicopters waiting to fly you to 
the Englefield Bay Lodge.  The 
chopper flight is nothing less than 
stunning.  You will be flying through 
deep ravines that are some of the 
most picturesque places on this earth.  
This part of the trip is jaw dropping.  
This is even before you get a fishing 
rod in your hand out on the edges of 
the Pacific Ocean.  That's just for 
starters and it only gets better from 
there.  
The chopper lands at the lodge, not 
just at the lodge but on a heli-pad 
connected to the floating lodge.  All 
the staff is lined up and ready to greet 
you and shake your hand as you get 
off the chopper.  The staff is not just 
going through the motions; they are 
eagerly waiting to assist you and fish 
with you for the next few days.  There 
is lunch and snacks waiting for you the 
minute you arrive.  No lines to wait in 
or any other inconveniences.  Boom.  
Eat your lunch.  Your bags are waiting 
for you at your room by the time lunch 
is done.  At this point the whole focus 
is to get you fed and to get you fishing 
as soon as possible. 
 Boats and fishing instructors are 
already assigned on a board.  Look at 
the board, go downstairs and get your 
rain pants, boots and rain parkas on.  
Rain gear and boots are supplied for 
you at the lodge.  Don't bring your rain 
gear.  The rain gear and boots are 
waiting for you in a well heated room 
and your name will be displayed next 
to your gear.  Get your gear on and 
head out to your boat.
The boat is ready to go.  A bait box full 
of brined herring, new hooks and 
leaders, rods, reels and everything 
else that you need to go fishing.  Most 
of the fishing reels are Islander Reels 
and most of the rods are 10 foot 
Shimano Talora fishing rods.  All the 
reels are filled with new line up to 
capacity.  There is no scrimping on 
second class gear.  All the gear is first 
rate.  If you want to bring your own 
fishing tackle as I do, feel free to do so.
The Lodge is in a sheltered inlet 
twenty minutes from the ocean.  
Once you board your boat with your 
fishing partner, you head on out to the 
ocean to fish for salmon on the first 
day of fishing.  
Tom Nelson and I were on the second 
plane from Vancouver this year, when 
we arrived at the Lodge people that 
were on the first plane had already 
caught their Chinook limits for that 
day.  As we were getting ready to head 
out fishing I thought that we had 
already missed the “hot” bite.  That's 
fishing?  Not so much.  
When Tom and his son Matt and I got 
out to the Ocean by the edge of the 
first reef, the Chinook were on a 
feeding frenzy.  At first we would pull 
our gear in because one of us would 
be fighting a salmon. Then before long 
we just left all the gear in the water 
because it would be two fish at once 
just about every hook up.  Always, 
two Chinook on at a time and it never 
stopped until it was time to go in for 
the day.  We caught quick limits of 
Chinook the first day after releasing 
many smaller 10-15lb Chinook that 
we did not want to bring home.  
Picture this: we left the lodge at 1 PM 
and we were back in time for dinner at 
the Lodge at 6 PM with full limits of 15 
to 25-pound Chinook.
When we arrived back at the Lodge, 
the crew was there to assist us with 
our fish.  If we wanted pictures, the 
dock crew laid the fish out or hung 
them on a scale for pictures.  From 
there we never touched the fish again.  
The dock crew gathered all the fish 
and took them to another crew that 
cleaned, fillet, cut and vacuum packed 
all the fish.  From there the fish are 
frozen.  Because of the huge volume 
of fish, there is a crew that works all 
night preparing the fish while you are 
sleeping.
On day two Tom, Matt and I decided 
that we will catch as many of our 
Halibut, Ling Cod and Yellow Eye Rock 
Fish that we can legally take that day.  
Judging by the year before, I thought 
that we would fish for at least a half 
day or more.  To my surprise, the 
fishing for all the bottom fish was as 
good as the salmon fishing.  By noon 
we had three halibut, nine Lingcod 
and nine Yellow Eye Rock Fish.  We 
had so many fish in the boat that we 
had to go back to the Lodge to unload 
our catch.  The boat had no more 
capacity for any more fish.  We 
probably had close to 300 pounds of 
fish in the boat.  What a haul!
After we dropped off our fish and ate 
lunch we were primed for Chinook 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
fishing.  The Ocean was really rough 
that afternoon.  There was a northerly 
wind blowing at least 20 miles per 
hour.  Needless to say, the water was 
really sloppy on the way out to the 
fishing grounds.  Even with a 20MPH 
Northerly wind, the Ocean is rough 
but you can get out and fish for 
salmon without feeling threatened.  
The fishing that afternoon was exactly 
like it was the day before and maybe 
even a notch or two better.  The 
fishing was so good we could barely 
get two rods in the water at one time.  
This went on as long as we could fish 
since the wind was steadily building.  
The salmon fishing was so incredible 
that we hated to leave.  Tom, Matt 
and I were the last boat on the water 
that day.  Now it was decision time to 
either continue fishing or hope that 
the fishing would be this good for one 
last day.  This caliber of Chinook 
fishing was pretty hard to leave 
because this day was a once in a life 
time salmon fishing experience.
At dinner after the second day of 
fishing, we were all hoping that the 
wind would lay down by morning and 
allow us a decent day on the water.
CATCH LIMITS
TOTAL POSSESSION
8 salmon, 2 halibut 6 lingcod, 6 red 
snapper
Daily Limits-based on 2-day limit
2 Chinook, 2 Coho, 3 lingcod, 3 red 
snapper
The weather on the third day of 
fishing was windy but tolerable in the 
morning.  Tom, Matt and I finished up 
our Chinook fishing with a couple fish 
in the mid-twenties.  The wind 
completely dissipated by late morning 
and now it was time to finish up with 
our Halibut, Ling Cod and Yellow Eye 
Rock fish.  After two hours of sorting 
through Halibut and Ling Cod it was 
time to take a break from reeling in 
fish non-stop.  There is a limit on how 
many times that you can let a line out 
to 200 to 250 feet of water and reel in 
fish.  Before long we had our 
possession limit of all the white fish 
that we needed.
That's the fishing aspect of Englefield 
Bay.  Now let's talk about the 
amenities of the Lodge.  The food at 
the Lodge is 5 Star.  Dinners will 
include steak or steak and lobster, fish 
or pasta.  The meals are cooked to 
perfection just like they would be at 
the best restaurant in Seattle.  Every 
morning there is fresh pastry, fresh 
baked cookies or brownies on the 
snack table.  There is also fresh fruit 
every day.  Even though the Lodge is in 
a very remote location there is always 
fresh fruit for breakfast and fresh 
vegetables at dinner.  Lunches are 
made and ready to take to your boat 
in the morning.  There is no waiting in 
line or any delays in the morning.  
Everything happens on time.  If you 
have an issue with anything the 
problems are remedied immediately 
with no questions asked.  
While you are out fishing on the 
Ocean and the bite is on, there is no 
going back to the lodge.  A hot lunch is 
brought for everyone out to an area 
near the edge of the Ocean.  You only 
have to go to the lunch boat to get 
your hot lunch if you choose to do so.  
The lunch boat will also pick up your 
fish and take the fish back to the 
Lodge for you.  That's service!
At the conclusion of your stay at 
Englefield Bay Lodge, your fish will be 
boxed and ready to go.  If the fishing is 
anything like it was during the last two 
years that I have been going, you 
should have two boxes with 50 
pounds of filleted fish in both boxes 
for a total of 100 pounds of fish all 
vacuum packed and ready to be put in 
your freezer when you arrive home.
THIS IS WHAT THE PACKAGE 
INCLUDES
1. Round Trip airfare from Vancouver BC 
to Sandspit via charted jet
2. Helicopter flight from Sandspit, BC to 
Englefield Bay Lodge
3. Deluxe accommodations based on 
double occupancy
4. All chef prepared meals, snacks and 
soft beverages
5. Fully equipped 18-foot center console 
boat with 90 horsepower Mercury 
outboard motors, maps, vhf radio, 
electric downriggers
6. Dawn to dusk fishing includes 5 hours 
guided fishing instruction per full day
7. All-weather gear, boots, and personal 
flotation collars
8. Cleaning, vacuum packing, flash 
freezing and boxing of your catch

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis                                 October 2016
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com
Chinook 
Fishing Seminar
November 4th, 7PM 
Bayside Marine 
1111 Craftsman Way, 
Everett 98201 
 
I will be having a Chinook Fishing 
Seminar November 4, 2016 at Bayside 
Marine.  The Seminar starts at 7PM.  My 
P o w e r P o i n t  C h i n o o k  f i s h i n g 
presentation will include some very 
useful information on how to become a 
successful salmon angler.  This seminar 
is for the most experienced salmon 
angler as well as the beginner.  If you 
pick up just a single nugget of 
information at my seminar your time 
should be well worth attending this free 
seminar.

See Page 3 for Details
Winter 
Crab Season?
The WDFW will announce new crabbing 
dates on/about October 1.  Hopefully 
by the time you read this Newsletter the 
winter crabbing season will be 
announced.  .Click here for crab seasons
Newsletter 
Mailing List
If you subscribed to the Newsletter 
mailing list in the last few months, you 
may have to do it again.  Anyone who 
subscribed to the Newsletter since May 
did not make it on to the mailing list.  I 
will let you know when I get this fixed. 
Chinook Fishing 
Resumes 
November 1
When November 1 arrives, we finally 
get some relief from all of the Puget 
Sound salmon closures that we have 
been dealing with since August.  
Chinook seasons are slated to open 
November 1 for Areas 8-1, 8-2, 9 and 10.  
Thank goodness we can get back to 
salmon fishing here on Puget Sound. 
 
Let's get a re-fresher course comparing 
winter Chinook to summer Chinook 
fishing.  This past summer there was an 
extraordinary amount of bait in Puget 
Sound, specifically at Possession Bar 
and at Kingston/Apple Tree Point.  
Because bait was so plentiful, there was 
good fishing for Chinook that were 
suspended at the top layers of the bait 
columns.  In fact, it was a relief not to 
bang the bottom while fishing for 
Chinook.  I believe that once we get 
back to fishing in November most of the 
bait will have gone elsewhere and we

will then have to rely on fishing tactics 
which paid off in the past.  Those 
tactics included fishing the edges in 90 
to 120 feet of water and fishing within 
5 to 10 feet of the bottom.  These 
basic Chinook fishing fundamentals 
should once again be rewarding when 
the season resumes. 
 
Puget Sound Chinook present in the 
winter months are wandering around 
looking for a meal.  These fish don't 
have an immediate destination as do 
summer Chinook.  If these winter 
Chinook are looking for bait, then so 
should we.  Many times starting in 
November bait will be scarce 
compared to summer months.  If you 
find bait, chances of catching Chinook 
will greatly increase. 
 
There are some simple rules to follow 
when you are fishing winter Chinook.  
One of the best rules to follow is find 
bait and then do what you can to stay 
in the vicinity of that bait.  Many times 
Chinook might not be present when 
you first locate the bait, but at some 
point in the tide the fish will either 
show up or go on the bite. Example:  
while I was Chinook fishing this 
summer on Possession Bar, I noticed a 
good Chinook bite came two hours 
before low tide.  There was plenty of 
bait present before the bite really 
came on, but the fish were either not 
in the mood to feed or they were not 
present during that two-hour period 
before the tide change.  Some days 
over half the fishermen left before the 
bite came on, especially when the bite 
was much later in the morning.  My 
point is this: exercise some patience 
and good judgement while waiting for 
a Chinook bite to start.  Once you find 
the bait the job gets easier! 
 Puget Sound is a big place and trying 
to hook a fish in this big body of water 
using a spoon that is only 3.5 inches in 
length is a daunting task.  Narrowing 
down the choices of places to fish is 
the essence of this Newsletter.  A 
person can waste a lot of hours 
trolling for Chinook without hooking 
up.  If you plan on being truly serious 
about Chinook fishing in Puget Sound, 
you must be dedicated to fishing 
along the defined edges of the many 
bar/sandy shoals that make up a very 
small percentage of areas here in 
Puget Sound.  Some of these areas 
include: Possession Bar, Apple Tree 
point, Point no Point, Mid Channel 
Bank, Pilot Point, Jeff Head, and 
Useless Bay.  These places to fish are 
just a fraction of the good areas to fish 
in the Central part of Puget Sound.  
However, these places I mentioned 
are where 90 per cent of all Chinook 
are caught in the Sound.  Want to 
n a r r o w  i t  d o w n  e v e n  m o r e ?  
Possession Bar is where the vast 
majority of Chinook are caught in 
Puget Sound followed by Mid Channel 
Bank and then Jeff Head.  Of course 
this can vary slightly from year to year 
and from month to month. 
In the November time frame, I 
recommend fishing Possession Bar, 
Jeff Head, Pilot Point and Useless Bay.  
These are my recommended fishing 
areas for winter Chinook.  Remember, 
tides come into play when fishing any 
of these areas.  You can't just go to any 
one of these spots because you 
caught a Chinook there the last time 
you were out.  That doesn't work very 
often. 
 
Possession Bar is one of the few 
fishing areas on my list where you can 
fish on most any tide.  When the tide 
is going out, I like Chinook fishing in 
what is called the “Tin Shed Drift” 
(check it on my maps).  Fishing the Tin 
Shed can also work when the tide is 
coming in but I prefer to go elsewhere 
in the winter months when hunting 
for Chinook. 
 
Jeff Head can be fished on either tide.  
Fish the South side of Jeff Head when 
the tide is coming in and fish the 
North side of Jeff Head when the tide 
is going out.  Nearby Jeff Head is 
Apple Tree Point.  I like fishing on the 
South side of that bar when the tide is 
coming in.  These are a few good 
choices if you are heading out of 
Shilshole or Edmonds Marina. 
 
A couple of places that I expect to 
catch a larger Chinook when the tide is 
coming are: Pilot Point or Useless Bay.  
These two places only produce fish on 
the flood tide.  Don't go to either one 
of these two places when the tide is 
going out. Period! 
 
You can see that you have to plan your 
November Chinook fishing in advance 
with a close look at a tide book in 
order to be successful.

Jeff Head 
Pilot Point 
Useless Bay  
 
The rigs for winter Chinook fishing are 
also a little different from summer 
Chinook fishing.  Plugs were fun to use 
in the summer.  That does not 
translate into good plug fishing for 
winter Chinook.  However, I would not 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
rule out 4 or 5 inch Tomic plugs for 
winter fishing.  If herring that are 
around in November are 6 inches and 
salmon are feeding on them, then 
plugs could be a smart choice. 
 
A safer bet to start with on November 
1 will be flashers and size 3.5-inch 
Kingfisher spoons.  Here is what I 
recommend having in my tackle 
collection before heading out. You can 
click on anyone one of these items to 
see a photo of each one or to 
purchase that item.  The shipping is 
free:  
 
Gibbs Flasher Red Racer 
UVGRMJRS 
Gibbs Flasher Purple Haze 
1PPUSUV 
Goldstar Kingfisher spoon 3.5 
#964 
Goldstar Kingfisher spoon 3.5 
#675 
Silver Horde Ace Hi Fly 
Chartreuse Spatter Back #140 
Tomic 5-inch Plug #602 or #603 
PLine CFX 30-pound 
Fluorocarbon leader 
Sampo X3CB Ball Bearing 
Snap Swivel 
 
Rigging Flashers
Rig the Kingfisher spoons so they are 
42 inches behind the flasher.  Tip: tie a 
l e n g t h  o f  3 0  p o u n d  P l i n e 
Fluorocarbon leader material to the 
spoon.  Snip the leader off at 46 
inches.  When the leader is tied to the 
flasher, it should be real close to 42 
inches in length.   
 
Rig an Ace Hi Fly 36 inches from the 
flasher.  Snip the leader off so that it is 
40 inches from the nose of the Ace Hi 
Fly.  When the leader is tied to the 
flasher, it will be close to 36 inches in 
length. 
 
Rigging Plugs
Plugs are simple to rig.  If the plug 
does not have a hook on it, put a 5/0 
Mustad siwash hook #9510XXXSS on 
the plug.  Some of the Tomic plugs 
come hook ready to fish.  Tie a 36-inch 
length of 30-pound fluorocarbon 
leader material to the plug.  Tie a 
Sampo X3RB swivel to the leader then 
tie the swivel to the fishing line. 
 
Trolling Speed
 
The beauty of using plugs and flashers 
at the same time, is that they can be 
trolled at the same speed.  The 
recommended trolling speed for 
Chinook should be 2.5 to 3.0 mph.  
Many times it is hard to conform to 
that tight range of trolling speeds. 
Sometimes an increase in speed or a 
decrease in speed is necessary just to 
keep the gear working.  A flasher is 
most effective when the downrigger 
cable is at a 45-degree angle.  As you 
know maintaining that 45-degree 
angle can be difficult during different 
stages of the tide.  This summer I 
found I had to troll at speeds between 
2.0 and 2.25 mph because I was 
fishing 150 to 200 feet deep.  I had to 
slow down just so that I could 
maintain my depth.  The point is this: 
There is an optimal speed then there 
is the speed you have to troll because 
of the tide and the depth combined. 
 
Everett 
Blackmouth Derby 
November 5 and 6
Tickets Available at John's 
Sporting Goods
 
The Bayside Salmon Derby which was 
traditionally held the first week in 
November, is now the Everett 
Blackmouth Derby.  This Blackmouth

Tickets are $30 per person.  Aside

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis                                    April 2017
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com
Halibut Seminar
by John Martinis
I will be giving a talk on Halibut fishing at 
the Everett Steelhead and Salmon Club 
April 20th @7PM.  You are invited to the 
talk that I am giving and the seminar is 
free to the public.  I will see you there!
Location: 2411 Hewitt Ave, Everett 
98201.  Map
Area 7 Chinook 
Opened March 25th
That’s correct, Marine Area 7 opened 
earlier than all of us anticipated on 
March 25.  Early reports suggest that 
the Chinook fishing is quite good in all 
the usual places
“The 2017 Halibut, 
Spot Shrimp and 
Lingcod Seasons” 
Opening Soon at an 
Area Near You 
 
Puget Sound Halibut Dates 
 
May 4, 6, and 11 and hopefully some 
other dates if the quota is not met 
during the three days of recreational 
fishing.  Halibut fishing, in most areas of 
Washington State, will open on the 
same three days. There are no size 
restrictions and the limit is one Halibut.  
Puget Sound 
Spot Shrimp 
  
There are no size restrictions and the 
limit is 80 Spot Shrimp 
 
Marine Area 6: Open May 6 and is open 
every day until the quota is achieved 
Marine Area 7 South:  Open May 6 
through May 21 
Marine Area 7 West:  Open May 6 and is 
open every day until the quota is 
achieved 
Marine Area 8-1: Open May 6 and 17 
Marine Area 8-2: Open May 6 and 17 
Marine Area 9:  Open May 6 and 17 
Marine Area 10: Open May 6 and 
another day to be considered later 
Marine Area 12:   Open May 6, 10, 17 
and 20 
 
Puget Sound Lingcod 
 
May 1 through June 15 
Size limit 26 inches to 36 inches 
 
Halibut Fishing 
 
Marine Areas 6, 7 and 9 
 
Halibut fishing in Marine Areas 6, 7, and 
9 is not for anglers wanting immediate 
gratification.  Halibut fishing can be and 
most often is more of a marathon run.  
To be successful at this sport in the 
Puget Sound Area you must be 
prepared to put in a lot of hours on the 
water.  The attraction of Halibut fishing 
Fishing Dates

based on quotas
and they

is that the fish can be 25 to 100 
pounds.  Even a 25-pound Halibut 
produces a heck of a lot of fillets.  My 
best advice to all new Halibut anglers 
is to be persistent and keep at it each 
day of the open season. 
 
Places to fish for Halibut are like 
salmon fishing areas. There are some 
relatively close fishing areas and then 
there some areas way out in the 
Straits of Juan de Fuca nowhere close 
to land.  So, choose the area that best 
fits your boat size. 
 
The best area in Area 9 to fish (if you 
don’t have a large enough boat or the 
experience of going out into the 
Straits) is Admiralty Bay.  There is a 
boat launch at Fort Casey near the 
ferr y terminal at the edge of 
Admiralty Bay.  From this boat launch 
you can be Halibut fishing in five 
minutes.   
 
From the Everett/Edmonds area, 
Mutiny Bay is probably a twenty-five-
minute run from either boat launch.  
Mutiny Bay is the closest place from 
either boat launch for a realistic 
chance for catching Halibut.  Because 
of Mutiny Bay’s proximity to the 
Seattle/Everett metropolitan area, it 
is also going to be the most crowded 
area to fish in Puget Sound.  Don’t let 
the crowds deter you because every 
year there are some nice Halibut 
caught out of Mutiny Bay. 
 
If your boat has a greater range and 
you have a sense of adventure, think 
about Halibut fishing at: Partridge 
Bank, Eastern Bank, Hein Bank 
McArthur Bank, Middle Bank and 
Coyote Bank.  
  
While salmon fishing in March I 
hooked and released a 40 pound 
Halibut on the Southwest corner of 
Partridge Bank and also caught and 
released a 25 pound Halibut on the 
Southeast corner of Coyote Bank.  The 
Halibut I caught at Partridge was in 
100 feet of water and the one I caught 
at Coyote was in 150 feet.  The 
Partridge Halibut was caught on a 
Coho killer and the Coyote Halibut 
was caught on a 5-inch herring.  
Wow…. sort of blows the theory 
about using large horse herring for 
catching Halibut??? 
 
The two most widely used methods 
for catching Halibut are: First - Drifting 
and pounding the bottom with 
spreader bars. Second - Anchoring 
and fishing close to the bottom with a 
spreader bar and bait or using a 
downrigger. 
 
Some Halibut anglers like to troll for 
Halibut with a 7 to 8-inch Herring 
placed off a downrigger.  When I 
started fishing for Halibut many years 
ago, I trolled for Halibut on Eastern 
Bank.  I used a dodger and a 7-inch 
herring and trolled slowly close to the 
bottom.  I caught as many Halibut 
then as I do now anchored to the 
bottom and waiting for a Halibut to 
ambush my Halibut rig. 
 
Let’s explore these two methods.  If 
y o u  a r e  u n c o m f o r t a b l e  w i t h 
anchoring your boat in 100 to 150 feet 
of water, the drifting method works 
just fine.  The largest Halibut I caught 
in the Straits was drifting on top of 
Partridge Bank in 60 feet of water.  On 
that day, I hooked a 100-pound 
Halibut and my brother-in-law Ernie 
got a Halibut that was around 50 
pounds. 
 
The Rig for Drifting for Halibut: I prefer 
to use an 18-inch spreader bar, a 7-
inch white Pline squid with two 10/0 
Gamakatsu octopus’ hooks. On the 
10/0 hooks, I tie a 7-inch herring on to 
the hooks with clear Miracle Thread. 
 
There are numerous ways to Halibut 
fish while on anchor.  Let’s look at a 
couple of ways to get correctly set-up: 
The spreader bar rig, as I described 
above, works quite well while on 
anchor.  An easier and likewise 
effective way to fish for Halibut while 
on anchor is to use a whole herring off 
a downrigger.  Rig the herring up just 
as you would for salmon fishing and 
drop it to within a few feet of the 
bottom.  When the tide/current slows 
down, you need to go back to the 
spreader bar method for about one 
hour while the current changes 
direction. If you do not heed my 
caution, you will experience one bad 
tangle-up that you could ever 
imagine.  While on anchor I would 
advise using a chum bag using either 
salmon parts or shrimp bait.  The bag 
can be zip-tied to the downrigger ball.  
Don’t make the chum bag too heavy 
since the weight could break the 
downrigger spool.  Five pounds of 
chum is more than enough to get the 
job done. 
 
Depths for Effective Halibut Fishing:  
Halibut can be caught at a depth from 
60 to 300 feet of water.  Remember, 
the greater the depth, the harder it is 
to keep bottom contact with the 
Halibut rig.  Here in the Puget Sound 
and the Straits of Juan de Fuca the 
sweet spot for Halibut fishing is about 
90 to 150 feet.

 If you do not want to tie your own 
Halibut rigs, I have the Pline 7-inch 
squid tied with 10/0 Gamakatsu 
hooks in the store.  I also package 
most of the items mentioned on the 
list below with two of everything in a 
large zip lock bag.

Halibut Seasons WDFW 
Recreational Spot 
Shrimp 
Harvesting Spot Shrimp is a ritual that 
a lot of shrimp fanatics participate in 
every year.  Yes, the Puget Sound 
shrimp season can be short if you are 
unwilling to look elsewhere after the 
two-day Puget Sound season has 
passed.  I will make sure that you get 
complete information on ways to 
expand your Spot Shrimp season.   
This is what your Spot Shrimp season 
could look like:  Harvest Spot Shrimp 
on Puget Sound May 6.  Then move to 
the San Juan’s for Spot Shrimp off 
Iceberg Point May 6 through 15.  On 
May 17 harvest Spot Shrimp in Puget 
Sound.  An alternative would be to go 
to Hood Canal on May 10 and harvest 
Spot Shrimp on that one day in Dabob 
Bay. After May 17 Areas 6 and 7 West 
are wide open.  Shrimping is open 
every day in these two Areas.  Hood 
Canal will open one more time on May 
20. The beauty of Hood Canal is that
you never need to worry about the 
current taking your gear away.  Areas 
7 South, 7 West and Area 6 are all tide 
dependent.  If there is more than six 
feet of exchange between any high or 
low tide, there is a possibility of losing 
your gear.  At $250 to $300 for a fully 
rigged shrimp pot, losing a shrimp pot 
gets your attention! 
A Fully Rigged Spot Shrimp Pot:  This 
should weigh at least 30 pounds.  
Most wire style shrimp pots only 
weigh 10 to 14 pounds.  Additional 
weights need to be added to the wire 
style pots.  The best placement of the 
weights is under the tunnels.  You can 
make or purchase a harness for the 
pot.  SMI makes a very sturdy four arm 
harness with an extra-large snap that 
will connect to any shrimp pot.  I like 
to attach the harness to the line with a 
stainless-steel oval.  Do not use a 
spring-loaded snap at this connection 
because the snap can easily come 
loose from the rope.  Sounds 
impossible but it happens.  From the 
oval attach, have at least 400 feet of 
rope.  The 400-foot chunk of rope 
should have a loop on each end.  The 
loops can be formed and clamped 
with hog rings and then wrapped with 
electrical tape. This makes for a very 
secure fitting.  At the surface end of 
the rope attach an oval that can then 
be attached to the yellow buoys.   
There are two ideas when it comes to 
the correct amount of floatation.  
Remember, the buoys are the only life 
line to your $250 pot.  Believe it or 
not, the buoys are where people like 
to cut costs - the very thing that 
protects your investment!  The 
correct amount of floatation for 
Marine Areas 8-1, 8-2, 9 and 12: Are 
two magnum solid foam yellow 
buoys.  The correct amount of 
flotation for Marine Areas 6 and 7: 
One Polyform inflatable buoy, either 
LD2 or A2 and two small solid foam 
yellow buoys.  Spend a day at John’s 
Sporting Goods and hear the horror 
stories of people losing four fully 
rigged Spot Shrimp pots.  Goodbye to 
$1000 plus (which, by the way, is not 
tax deductible). It often happens, 
especially off Iceberg Point on the 
south end of Lopez Island.  This is the 
“Bermuda Triangle” grave yard for lost 
shrimp pots.  
If you make your buoys and line 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
detachable with stainless steel ovals, 
you can adjust the buoys to the needs 
of where you are going shrimping. 
5/16-inch leaded rope or ¼ inch 
leaded rope? 
I prefer ¼ inch leaded rope for several 
reasons: ¼ inch rope coils much easier 
than 5/16-inch rope.  ¼ inch rope 
costs significantly less than 5/16-inch 
rope.  Four 400 foot shots of ¼ inch 
rope will fit into one large 18-gallon 
bucket.  The only drawback to ¼ inch 
rope is that you have to hold on to the 
rope tighter while the shrimp pot 
puller is pulling the line in.  No big deal 
because only one rope/pot can be 
retrieved at a time.  The major reason 
for using ¼ inch rope is because it has 
less drag in the water.  This is a big deal 
when shrimping in Areas 6 and 7. 
Mixing Spot Shrimp Bait 
If you look at newsletters I have 
written in the past, you notice I 
r e c o m m e n d e d  k e e p i n g  t h e 
components of the shrimp bait 
separate.   Yes, it continues to work 
quite well.  However, in the past 
several years, I began mixing my bait 
in five-gallon buckets using a five-
gallon paint mixer attached to a drill.  
The basic shrimp bait ingredients are:  
Canned Mackerel 
Shrimp Bait Pellets 
Friskies Ocean whitefish 
Tuna Pate cat food 
Pro Cure Crab and shrimp attractant   
Unfortunately, Ace of Baits shrimp oil 
is no longer made.  
Pour 5 pounds of Pellets in a five-
gallon bucket 
Add 2 to 4 cans of Mackerel 
including the juice 
Add 4 cans of cat food 
Add two cups of bait oil 
Keep some oatmeal handy in case the 
mixture becomes too liquid.  Adding a 
cup or two of oatmeal will thicken the 
shrimp bait.  This mixing should be 
done the night prior to shrimping. This 
will give the pellets time to absorb all 
the liquids.  Check the bait the next 
day and make certain it has the 
consistency of peanut butter.  If the 
bait is the correct consistency, it 
should bleed out of the bait container 
at the rate of 50 % after a one hour pot 
soak. 
I prefer using two of the 9 inch SMI 
bait tubes per pot.  After a one hour 
pot soak I remove all the bait from the 
containers into an empty bucket and 
put fresh bait in the tubes.  Then, I 
save the used bait for later in the day 
or for another day of shrimping.  The 
used bait can be refreshed by adding 
more key ingredients that I previously 
mentioned.  Last year when the Spot 
Shrimp limit was doubled in Area 6, I 
used the refreshed bait that I had used 
earlier in the day.

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis                                    August 2017
John’s Sporting Goods Web Page www.johnssportinggoods.com
Transition Time
Now that Marine Area 9 is closed we 
now move on to “Part Two” of the Puget 
Sound Chinook salmon season.  
Yes indeed, Area 9 was a barn burner 
especially at Mid Channel Bank at Port 
Townsend.   I believe many of you will 
agree that fishing at Mid Channel was 
probably the best Chinook fishing in 
Puget Sound in the last 25 years or 
more.  With Area 9 in the history books 
don't despair, there is still a lot of good 
Chinook fishing ahead.
So, this is how it works:  When Area 9 
closes the migrating masses of Chinook 
being caught by you, me and everyone 
else will now shoot through Area 9 with 
a large portion of the group heading to 
Area 10.  In fact, for a couple of days, 
there should be an immediate uptick in 
Area 10 Chinook catches after Area 9 
closes.  
Marine Area 10 description: From Apple 
Cove Point-Edwards Point to a line 
projected true east-west through the 
north tip of Vashon Island.
Emergency Regulation: Increases the 
daily limit for hatchery Chinook to two 
fish in Marine Area 10, excluding 
Sinclair Inlet and fishing piers. Effective 
Date: 12:01 a.m. Saturday, July 29th, 
through 11:59 p.m. Tuesday, August 
15th, 2017.
There are three key Chinook fishing 
areas in Area 10: Richmond Beach, 
Presidents Head (Jeff Head) and 
Kingston.  Last year I fished extensively 
at Kingston for Chinook and did quite 
well.
Kingston:  I like to start fishing back 
inside the bay at Kingston just north of 
the ferry lanes.  There is a well-defined 
bar I follow in 90 to 100 feet of water.  
Follow the bar to the east to a point 
where it turns north.  When you get to 
that point, turn around and troll back 
into the bay.  Some anglers like to troll 
deep inside the bay at Kingston back to 
the ferry lanes.
Tackle that I would recommend for 
Kingston Chinook
Gibbs Red Racer flasher
Coho Killer spoon #395 Herring Aide
Coho Killer spoon #675 
Cookies n Cream
3.5 Kingfisher spoon #395 Herring Aide
There is a decent chance Sand Lance 
and Herring will be present at Kingston 
so prepare to use larger spoons than 
you were using at Mid Channel Bank or 
Possession Bar. I recommend fishing 
Kingston only on the flood tide.  Note: 
grass and sea weed can be intolerable at 
times at Kingston.
Jeff Head (President Point): Jeff Head is 
the “go to” Chinook and Coho fishing 
Area in Central Puget Sound.  This area 
is relatively easy to fish.  Start trolling at 
Jeff Head (Jefferson head) and troll to 
the Southwest.  Navigate your way into 
90 to 120 feet of water.  The bar will 
curve slightly to the West into Port

Madison.  As you round Jeff head, it 
has some nice structure where the 
bait and salmon are sometimes hiding 
close to the bar.  Troll into Port 
Madison for one-half mile and then 
turn and troll back to Jeff Head.  I 
would recommend trolling out as far 
as the 150-foot line if the bait is not 
pushed up to the side of the bar in 90 
to 120 feet of water.
Tackle that I would recommend for

Coho Killer spoon #395 Herring Aide

So again, there is a chance that Sand 
Lance and Herring will be present at 
Jeff Head so be prepared to use a 
larger spoon than used at Mid 
Channel Bank or Possession Bar.
I would recommend fishing Jeff Head 
on the ebb tide.  However, at times 
this area can be productive on both 
the ebb and the flood tide.  If the grass 
and sea weed is unmanageable at 
Kingston, go directly to Jeff Head. 
Point Wells/Richmond Beach: This 
area can be fished on either tide.  If 
the tide is ebbing (going out), start 
fishing one mile south of Edwards 
Point and troll back to Edwards Point.  
If the tide is flooding, I would start 
trolling at Edwards Point and troll one 
mile south.  My recommendation 
would be to troll in one direction only 
depending on which way the water is 
moving. Fish in about 90 to 120 feet of 
water. The suggested tackle is the 
same as mentioned for Jeff Head and 
Kingston.
Elliot Bay Special Chinook Fishery 
August 11th to 13th:  Elliot Bay has 
not been opened for Chinook fishing 
for a long time.  And when it does 
open, it will be open for three days 
only so you better “get on it” from day 
one.  A word of advice for fishing Elliot 
Bay, “Early”.  You must be on the 
water before daylight to effectively 
participate in this downtown Seattle 
Chinook fishery.  There is a light-
switch Chinook bite at daylight and 
you better be there at the crack of 
dawn to get your fish!
Elliot Bay Special Regulations:  
Chinook - minimum size 22 inches. 
Other Salmon species - no minimum 
size. Daily limit 2 (combined). Release 
all Chum and wild Coho.

Marine Area 7 
Chinook
August 1st, One Chinook Limit 
hatchery or wild. Marine area 7 has 
two distinct summer Chinook runs 
that travel through the Islands at 
different times and different places.  
The early run starts well before Area 7 
opens on July 1st.  These Chinook are 
mainly Fraser River Spring Chinook.  
Because of the strong run size this 
year, the Spring Chinook fishery in 
Area 7 lasted to the end of July.  Most 
years the run fades out after July 15th.
The next run of Summer Chinook 
through the San Juan Islands begins 
around the first week of August and 
should last into September.  These 
salmon are a mix of Fraser River and 
Samish River Chinook.  We should see 
these salmon showing up on the west 
side of San Juan Island at Eagle Point 
near the end of the first week in 
August.
I prefer to fish Eagle Point on the last 
half of the ebb tide.  This is a simple 
place to fish.  The water is deep close 
to shore.  Unlike Puget Sound, you 
don't have to fish close to the bottom 
for Chinook in this area.  I prefer to 
fish in 60 to 120 feet of water and set 
my gear at 50 to 60 feet.  Some years I 
catch my Chinook trolling an Anchovy 
Shellfish Hotline 1-866-880-5421
behind a flasher or by trolling a whole 
herring.  Other years, I use Coho Killer 
or Kingfisher 3.5 spoons.  The theory 
behind using this type of gear is the 
presence of Herring or Sand Lance.  
The only way to get a definitive 
answer regarding what bait the fish 
are feeding on is open one up to see 
what's inside the fish.
Area 7 Rules: Chinook  – minimum 
size 22 inches. Other Salmon species - 
no minimum size. Daily limit 2 
(combined) plus 2 additional Sockeye. 
Only 1 Chinook may be retained. 
Release all Coho and Chum.

Eagle Point Chinook
Closer to Home  - One more note on 
Chinook fishing. Don't miss out on the 
Tulalip Bubble. Last year the Chinook 
fishing was quite good in August.  The 
day before I started writing this 
Newsletter, the Everett Boat Launch 
fish checker said more Chinook were 
checked in from the Bubble than 
anywhere else that day.  That was 
either the last Friday or Saturday in 
July.
Coho Fishing Open 
from the Shore in 
Prescribe Areas of 
Marine Areas 
8-2 and 9
Area 8-2:  August 1st to September 
4th: Possession Point Fishery: Waters 
from Possession Point to the northern 
b o r d e r  o f  P o s s e s s i o n  B e a c h

fishing only. Fishing from any floating 
device is prohibited.
Area 9: August 1st to September 4th: 
No minimum size. Daily limit 2 
(combined). Release Chinook, Chum, 
and wild Coho. Shoreline fishing only. 
Fishing from any floating device is 
prohibited.  See pages 114 and 115 in 
the Rule Book for specific rules 
regarding shoreline fishing for Coho 
during this time.
If you want to participate in the 
Coho Shoreline fishery, this is the 
proper gear:
8 ½ to 9-foot Lamiglas X11 Medium 
action graphite rod will work 
2.5 Pink or Green Holographic Buzz 
Bombs or Green or Pink Rotators  
#7 black barrel swivels

You could also fish with a float and 4 to 
5-inch herring. If you plan to drive to 
Whidbey Island to fish from the beach 
for Hatchery Coho check out the 
sailing schedule for the Mukilteo to 
Clinton Ferry, Click Here.
From WDFW
Marine Area 9 salmon anglers limited 
to shoreline fishing July 31; Chinook 
retention closes
Action: Closes Marine Area 9 
(Admiralty Inlet) to chinook retention, 
and restricts salmon anglers to 
shoreline fishing only.
Effective Date: Effective 12:01 a.m., 
Monday, July 31, 2017
Species affected: Chinook salmon.
Location: Puget Sound, Marine Area 9 
(Admiralty Inlet Area).
Reason for action: Preliminary 
estimates through Thursday indicate 
that anglers had caught 4,642 fish (83 
percent) of the chinook quota of 
5,599 fish for Marine Area 9. WDFW 
anticipates reaching the quota for this 
fishery by the end of the day Sunday. 
The changes to the chinook fishery 
are in compliance with conservation 
o b j e c t i v e s  a n d  a g r e e d - t o
management plans.
In addition, Marine Area 9 will remain 
open to salmon fishing only from the 
shoreline. Anglers will not be 
permitted to fish for salmon from a 
boat or other floating device starting 
Monday (July 31). The reason for this 
action is to protect expected low runs 
of wild coho and pink salmon

Information For The Serious Angler              by John Martinis February 2017

Seminar 2017
By John Martinis
Chinook Seminar
Wednesday March 15th
at Bayside Marine @7PM
1111 Craftsman Way, Everett
You are invited, free to the public
My popular Chinook seminar will be 
held on March 15.  I will be presenting 
winning strategies guaranteed to put 
more Chinook in your boat. I will talk 
about correct methods to rig flashers 
and spoons as well as fishing with 
herring.  In addition, we will go over 
some fishing charts that should help 
getting to the correct fishing spot on the 
right tide.  Take the guesswork out 
Chinook fishing and be at the seminar at 
Bayside Marine on March 15 at 7 PM.
The Everett Steelhead and Salmon Club 
will have a raffle at the end of the 
seminar. There will be some great prizes 
including rods, reels,and salmon tackle.

Planning and 
Executing a Chinook 
Fishing Trip to 
Marine Area 6
When January rolled around everyone, 
including myself, was eagerly waiting 
th
for Area 9 to open on January 16  the 
published opening date.  No such luck.  
Well, January 16th has come and gone 
and Area 9 is still closed for Chinook 
because of emergency regulations.  We 
will save that debate for another date. 
It's time to move on.
When special salmon closures occur, I 
don't just sit at the dock and lament the 
closings.  Salmon closures are just a fact 
of life in Puget Sound these days and we 
need to work around these issues.  
Now, I am looking at the fishing 
possibilities for Marine Areas 6 and 7.  Is 
it too far to go?  Closures now force me 
to look elsewhere for any salmon fishing 
prospects.   We have entered a new age 
for scheduling fishing trips.  Now the 
planning includes hitting the road or 
going by boat to those Areas which are 
still open for Salmon.  These places are 
not too far away and no your boat is not 
too small.  Proper planning and 
observing weather conditions are key 
when traveling to either Area 6 or 7.
I usually do not use the Newsletter to 
talk about my recent fishing trips 
around Puget Sound.  Normally, I use
